checklist: uses at least 2 clues from lines 5 to 8
explains the physical discomfort of the cold
explains the feelings of being told off or feeling inferior
questions.explanation: The best answers use words around dreadful to explain the reasons, rather than just giving a synonym such as awful.

units.title: Reading between the lines
units.summary: Explicit information is stated; implicit information is suggested. An inference is only as strong as the evidence you point to.

questions.prompt: Which of these is stated directly in the text (explicit)?
options: The lady was dressed in black.
The lady fears for her life.
The lady has travelled a long way.
questions.explanation: Line 1 says she is “dressed in black”. The other ideas may be true, but you would have to infer them.

questions.prompt: Who is telling this story? Use the words “as we entered” (line 1) and what Holmes says in lines 2 to 3 to work it out.
questions.explanation: The narrator says “we entered”, and Holmes introduces “my intimate friend and associate, Dr. Watson”, so Watson must be narrating.

questions.prompt: Holmes speaks “cheerily” (line 2). What does this suggest about him when he meets the lady?
options: He is welcoming and in good spirits.
He is annoyed at being disturbed.
He is too tired to listen.
questions.explanation: Cheerily shows a bright, friendly manner, which fits his offer of the fire and hot coffee.

questions.prompt: Why does the lady change her seat (lines 6 to 7)?
options: Holmes has asked her to sit nearer the fire.
She wants to sit by the window.
questions.explanation: She changes her seat “as requested”, and Holmes had just said “Pray draw up to it”, meaning the fire.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 details that suggest the lady is in great distress.
questions.explanation: Drawn, frightened and haggard all suggest someone worn out by fear. Sitting in the window and a polite greeting tell us nothing about her feelings.

questions.prompt: She arrives “heavily veiled” (line 1). What is the best inference about why?
options: She may want to hide her face, her fear or who she is.
Holmes asked all visitors to wear veils.
questions.explanation: When she raises the veil we see her “pitiable state of agitation”, so the veil may have hidden her distress. The text gives no evidence for the other options.

questions.prompt: She was “in a pitiable state of agitation” (lines 9 to 10). What does agitation mean?
questions.explanation: Agitation means being troubled and unable to stay calm, which fits her “restless frightened eyes”.

questions.prompt: Holmes is glad that “Mrs. Hudson has had the good sense to light the fire” (line 4). What can you infer from this?
options: Mrs Hudson looks after the house, and Holmes approves of what she has done.
Mrs Hudson is the lady in black.
questions.explanation: Holmes praises Mrs Hudson's “good sense”, which suggests she runs the household and has prepared the room.
questions.misconception: Guessing an inference that the words do not support.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false, using evidence from the text.

statements.s: The lady is about 30 years old.
Holmes guesses correctly why she is shivering.
Watson is a stranger to Holmes.
Holmes wants the lady to feel comfortable.

questions.explanation: She has the figure of “a woman of thirty”; Holmes thinks she is cold but she says “It is not cold which makes me shiver”; Watson is Holmes's “intimate friend”; Holmes offers the fire and coffee.

questions.prompt: What impression does Conan Doyle create of the lady before she tells her story? Make 2 inferences and support each with evidence.
questions.model: The lady seems terrified: she says “It is fear, Mr. Holmes. It is terror.”, and her eyes are “like those of some hunted animal”, as if something is chasing her. She also seems to have suffered for a long time, because she is only about 30 but her expression is “weary and haggard”, which suggests many sleepless nights.
checklist: makes 2 clear inferences about the lady
supports each inference with a short quotation
explains how the evidence leads to the inference
questions.explanation: Each inference should be tied to the exact words that suggest it.

units.title: Choosing and using quotations
units.summary: Short quotations copied exactly work best. Fit each one into your own sentence so that the sentence still reads smoothly.

questions.prompt: You want to show that things in the room have aged. Which is the best short quotation?
options: “It was not in the first few moments that I saw all these things”
“the rounded figure of a young woman”
questions.explanation: A single word can be enough. Yellow shows white things have discoloured with age; the long quotation says nothing about ageing.

questions.prompt: Which of these is copied exactly from line 3?
questions.explanation: The text says “lost its lustre”, with British spelling and no apostrophe in its.
questions.misconception: Changing spelling or grammar when copying a quotation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence embeds a quotation most smoothly?
options: Pip sees that the bride has “withered like the dress”, as if she has dried up with it.
Pip says, “I saw that the bride within the bridal dress had withered like the dress, and like the flowers”. This shows she is old.
questions.explanation: The first sentence fits a short quotation into the writer's own sentence and explains it straight away.

questions.prompt: Complete the quotation accurately. The figure had “shrunk to ___ and bone” (lines 6 to 7).
questions.explanation: The full phrase is “shrunk to skin and bone”, an idiom for someone extremely thin.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes that Miss Havisham's eyes are “bright”, so she seems lively. Why is this misleading?
options: The text says the only brightness left was in her “sunken eyes”, which suggests illness, not life.
The word bright is not in the text at all.
Dickens says her eyes are closed.
The pupil should have used a longer quotation.
questions.explanation: Quoting a word out of its context can reverse the meaning. Sunken eyes are a sign of age or illness.
questions.misconception: Taking a word out of context so that it no longer means what the writer meant.

questions.prompt: Tick the 2 quotations that best support the idea that Miss Havisham seems hardly alive.
questions.explanation: Skin and bone, and waxwork and skeleton, both suggest a body close to death. The other quotations are not about her.

questions.prompt: Put these quotations in the order they appear in the extract.
questions.explanation: Dickens moves from the dress and room to Miss Havisham's body, then to Pip's memories of the waxwork and the skeleton.

questions.prompt: Which is the best comment on the word “withered” (line 4)?
options: It suggests she has dried up like a dying flower, as if her life drained away while she waited.
It makes the reader want to read on.
questions.explanation: The best comment explores the connotations of the word and links it to her situation. Simply saying old is a synonym, not an explanation.
questions.misconception: Giving a synonym instead of exploring what a word suggests.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each rule for using quotations is true or false.

statements.s: Quotations must be copied exactly.
A longer quotation always earns more credit.
You can change a word in a quotation if it reads better.
A quotation can be a single word.

questions.explanation: Examiners reward short, exact quotations that are explained. Changing the words means it is no longer a quotation.

questions.prompt: Write 2 sentences explaining how Dickens makes Miss Havisham frightening. Embed 2 short quotations.
questions.model: Dickens makes Miss Havisham frightening by showing that she has “shrunk to skin and bone” inside a dress made for a young woman, so she looks like a body that has wasted away. Pip even compares her to a “waxwork and skeleton” whose “dark eyes” still move, which is more terrifying than a corpse because she is alive.
checklist: 2 short quotations copied exactly
quotations embedded in the writer's own sentences
an explanation of why each detail is frightening
questions.explanation: Keep quotations short and let your own words do the explaining.

units.title: Summarising
units.summary: A summary gives the main points briefly in your own words. Leave out examples and small details, and keep the focus of the question as the subject of your sentences.

questions.prompt: What is the extract mainly about?
options: how giant tortoises find and drink water
how Darwin travelled to the islands
questions.explanation: Almost every sentence is about the tortoises' need for water and how they reach it.

questions.prompt: According to lines 1 to 3, where are the springs found?
options: only on the larger islands, towards the centre and high up
on every island, near the beach
questions.explanation: Lines 1 to 2 say “The larger islands alone possess springs”, which are “towards the central parts, and at a considerable height”.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 statements that are main points rather than minor details.
options: Tortoises love water and drink a great deal.
Springs are only found high up on the larger islands.
The Spaniards found the watering-places by following the paths.
A tortoise swallows about 10 mouthfuls a minute.
Tortoises from low ground travel long distances to drink.
questions.explanation: The Spaniards and the exact drinking rate are interesting details, but the summary still makes sense without them.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of lines 9 to 11?
options: At the spring, a tortoise drinks greedily and ignores anyone watching.
questions.explanation: Lines 9 to 11 describe the tortoise burying its head and swallowing “great mouthfuls” while “regardless of any spectator”.

questions.prompt: You are summarising what the tortoises do. Which sentence keeps the right focus?
options: The tortoises travel long distances to reach the springs.
Darwin was amazed when he landed.
Chatham Island is in the Pacific.
questions.explanation: Making the tortoises the subject of each sentence keeps a summary on task.
questions.misconception: Writing about the writer or other people instead of the subject the question asks about.

questions.prompt: Darwin says tortoises “can subsist” (line 15) where little rain falls. What does subsist mean?
questions.explanation: To subsist is to stay alive with very little. The sentence is about living with almost no water.

questions.prompt: Put these main points in the order Darwin gives them.
items: The springs are high up in the middle of the larger islands.
Well-worn paths lead from the springs to the coast.
At the spring a tortoise drinks huge amounts.
Tortoises can survive with only a little rain.
questions.explanation: Following the writer's order helps a summary stay accurate.

questions.prompt: Check your understanding. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Every island has springs.
Tortoises living on low ground must travel to drink.
The local people agreed about how often tortoises visit the water.
Some tortoises live where rain is the only water.

questions.explanation: Only the larger islands have springs; the inhabitants “differed respecting the frequency of these visits”; and tortoises can live where water only “falls during a few rainy days in the year”.

questions.prompt: A pupil's summary includes this sentence: The tortoises swallow about 10 mouthfuls a minute, which Darwin noticed at Chatham Island. What is wrong with it for a summary?
options: It includes minor details and exact figures instead of the main point.
questions.explanation: A summary would simply say that tortoises drink large amounts quickly. The figure and place are details.
questions.misconception: Copying examples and figures into a summary.

questions.prompt: Summarise in 2 or 3 sentences what lines 11 to 16 tell us about how often tortoises visit water and how they survive. Use your own words.
questions.model: Local people say that each tortoise stays near the water for a few days and then goes back to lower ground, although they disagree about how often this happens. Darwin thinks the tortoises' food decides how often they need to drink, and he is sure they can live on islands where rain is the only water.
checklist: covers the length of a visit and the disagreement about how often
includes Darwin's view about food and survival with little rain
uses own words and leaves out minor detail
questions.explanation: Keep each sentence about the tortoises and put the ideas in your own words.

units.title: Purpose, audience and context
units.summary: Ask why a text was written and who it is for. The vocabulary and the way the reader is addressed are your best clues.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Text C?
questions.explanation: Text C gives rules: visitors must sign in and wear a lanyard.

questions.prompt: Who is Text B most likely written for?
questions.explanation: The casual style, the kiss and “save me a slice” show it is for someone close.

questions.prompt: Match each text to its main purpose.
pairs: to persuade people to donate old bikes
to let someone know about a delay
to give an opinion on a café
questions.explanation: Each text's purpose shapes its language: A persuades, B informs, C instructs and D reviews.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 features that show Text B is informal.
questions.explanation: Missing capitals, doubled exclamation marks and a kiss all belong to a quick, friendly message.

questions.prompt: Which word in Text C shows that signing in is a rule, not a suggestion?
questions.explanation: Must shows something is required. Please is polite and softens the second instruction.

questions.prompt: Text A begins “Got an old bike gathering dust?” Why does it start with a question?
options: to speak directly to readers and make them think of their own bike
because the writer does not know the answer
to show that bikes are dusty
questions.explanation: A direct question involves the reader straight away, which suits a persuasive leaflet.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The writer of Text D has probably visited the café.
Text A is aimed at people who have a spare bike.
Text C is aimed at pupils who already know the school.
Text B was carefully planned and checked.

questions.explanation: Text D judges the pancakes and queue from experience; Text A asks people with old bikes to donate; Text C is for visitors; Text B is dashed off.

questions.prompt: Where would Text C most likely be displayed?
questions.explanation: Its audience is visitors, who first arrive at reception.

questions.prompt: Text D says the weekend queue “tests your patience”. Why might the reviewer include a criticism?
options: to seem fair and balanced, so readers trust the praise
questions.explanation: A review that mentions a weakness sounds honest, which makes its recommendation more believable.
questions.misconception: Thinking a text with a criticism must be against the thing it reviews.

questions.prompt: Explain how the writer of Text A suits the language to its audience and purpose. Refer to 2 features.
questions.model: Text A is meant to persuade local people to give away old bikes, so it speaks to them directly with a question, “Got an old bike gathering dust?”, which makes readers picture their own unused bike. It then uses imperatives such as “Bring it” and ends with the slogan “Every bike counts!”, so the reader feels that even one donation will help a family.
checklist: identifies the purpose and audience
explains 2 features with short quotations
links each feature to how it persuades
questions.explanation: Say what each feature does for this audience, not just what it is called.

units.title: Word choice and connotations
units.summary: Ask why the writer chose this word and not another. Think about its connotations, the ideas and feelings it carries, and say what it adds.

questions.prompt: Wuthering Heights is Mr Heathcliff's “dwelling” (line 1). What is a dwelling?
questions.explanation: A dwelling is a place where someone lives. It is a slightly formal word.

questions.prompt: The windows are narrow and “deeply set in the wall” (line 7). What is the most likely reason?
options: to protect the house from the wind
questions.explanation: The whole passage is about the power of the wind, so the windows are built to resist it.

questions.prompt: The corners are “defended with large jutting stones” (line 7). What does the word defended suggest?
options: The house is like a castle under attack.
questions.explanation: Defended belongs to the language of battle, so the house seems to be fighting the weather.

questions.prompt: Lockwood mentions “Pure, bracing ventilation” (line 3). What does bracing mean here?
questions.explanation: Bracing air is sharp and cold enough to wake you up.

questions.prompt: What is Lockwood's tone when he says “Pure, bracing ventilation they must have up there at all times”?
questions.explanation: He describes a violent wind as if it were a pleasant feature, which is a joke by understatement.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 words or phrases that belong to a semantic field of battle or strength.
questions.explanation: Defended, power and strong together make the house and the wind sound like opponents in a fight.

questions.prompt: The thorns are “stretching their limbs one way” (line 5). What does the word limbs suggest?
options: The bushes are like human bodies with arms.
questions.explanation: Limbs usually means arms and legs, so the thorns seem human, reaching out.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes: The word excessive shows there is a lot of slant. Why is this a weak comment?
options: It only repeats the meaning. A better answer says the trees lean far more than normal, proof of the wind's force.
Excessive is not in the text.
The pupil should name a technique first.
questions.explanation: A strong comment explores what the word suggests rather than giving a synonym.
questions.misconception: Explaining a word by repeating its dictionary meaning.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about connotations is true or false.

statements.s: “Happily” suggests Lockwood is glad the house is well built.
“jutting” suggests stones that stick out sharply.
“dwelling” sounds more casual than “house”.
“bracing” suggests warm and cosy air.

questions.explanation: Happily shows relief, and jutting suggests sharp edges. Dwelling is more formal than house, and bracing air is cold.

questions.prompt: How does Brontë's word choice make the setting of Wuthering Heights seem harsh? Explain the connotations of 2 words or phrases.
questions.model: Brontë makes the setting harsh by showing its effects on everything that grows there. The “excessive slant” of the firs suggests they have been forced over by a wind that never stops. The thorns are “craving alms of the sun”, like starving beggars, which suggests the place is so cold and bare that even plants are desperate for warmth. Even the house has to be “defended”, as if the weather were an enemy.
checklist: chooses 2 precise words or phrases
explores their connotations rather than giving synonyms
links the words to the harshness of the setting
questions.explanation: Focus on individual words and what they suggest.

units.title: Figurative language
units.summary: Similes, metaphors and personification are not meant literally. Ask what the comparison suggests about the thing being described.

questions.prompt: In line 1, which human quality does Chopin give the sea?
questions.explanation: “The voice of the sea” treats the sea as if it could speak.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 words in line 1 that describe the sounds of the sea's voice.
questions.explanation: Whispering, clamoring and murmuring all appear in line 1. Roaring and singing are not in the text.

questions.prompt: The voice of the sea is “seductive” (line 1). What does seductive mean here?
questions.explanation: Something seductive draws you towards it. The next words, “inviting the soul to wander”, support this.

questions.prompt: Chopin writes of “abysses of solitude” (line 2). What does this metaphor suggest?
options: a loneliness so deep it seems bottomless
questions.explanation: An abyss is a deep pit. Linking it to solitude makes being alone feel vast and endless.

questions.prompt: Thinking is compared to “mazes” in line 2. What does this suggest about Edna's thoughts?
options: They twist and turn, and she could get lost in them.
questions.explanation: A maze is easy to enter and hard to leave, so the sea draws the mind into confusing, inward thoughts.

questions.prompt: Which technique is used in “enfolding the body in its soft, close embrace” (lines 3 to 4)?
questions.explanation: Only a person can embrace, so the sea is given a human action.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The sea literally speaks words to Edna.
Chopin suggests the sea seems to call to Edna.
The embrace makes the sea seem comforting.
“mazes” means there are paths along the beach.

questions.explanation: Figurative language works through suggestion: the sea seems to call and comfort, but it does not really talk, and the mazes are in the mind.
questions.misconception: Reading figurative language literally.

questions.prompt: Chopin's list “whispering, clamoring, murmuring” mixes quiet and loud sounds. What is the effect?
options: The sea's voice seems constant and ever-changing, impossible to ignore.
It shows the sea is calm all the time.
It makes the passage confusing for no reason.
questions.explanation: The changing sounds, together with “never ceasing”, make the sea's call seem endless.

questions.prompt: Amir says “abysses of solitude” is a simile. Why is he wrong?
options: It uses no like or as; it describes solitude as if it were an abyss, so it is a metaphor.
It is personification because it mentions a soul.
It is a fact, not a comparison.
He is right; all comparisons are similes.
questions.explanation: A simile compares using like or as. This phrase states the comparison directly, so it is a metaphor.
questions.misconception: Calling every comparison a simile.

questions.prompt: How does Chopin use figurative language to make the sea seem both tempting and dangerous? Refer to 2 examples.
questions.model: Chopin personifies the sea as having a “seductive” voice that keeps “inviting the soul to wander”, so it seems to call Edna like a person she cannot resist. The embrace is “soft” and “close”, which is comforting, but the soul is invited into “abysses of solitude”, which suggests something deep and dark that she might not return from.
checklist: explains 2 examples of figurative language
shows how the sea seems tempting
shows how the same language hints at danger
questions.explanation: The strongest answers notice that the same images can be read in 2 ways.

units.title: Sound and pattern
units.summary: Alliteration, rhyme, rhythm and repetition shape how a poem sounds. Naming a device earns little; say what the sound or pattern does.

questions.prompt: The poem is written in rhyming couplets. Which word rhymes with “witches” (line 1)?
questions.explanation: Lines 1 and 2 rhyme: witches and ditches.

questions.prompt: Which phrase uses alliteration?
questions.explanation: Glimpse and gone repeat the g sound at the start of nearby words.

questions.prompt: “clambers and scrambles” (line 9) rhyme inside a single line. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Rhyme within one line is internal rhyme. It makes the line bounce, like the child scrambling.

questions.prompt: The horses and cattle are “charging along like troops in a battle” (line 3). What does the simile suggest?
options: The animals seem to rush past in lines, like soldiers.
The animals are fighting each other.
questions.explanation: From a fast train, fields of animals seem to charge by. The animals are not really moving fast; the train is.

questions.prompt: Which word begins lines 9, 11 and 13?
questions.explanation: The repeated “Here is” points out one sight after another.

questions.prompt: What is the effect of repeating “Here is” in the second half of the poem?
options: It is like pointing quickly at each sight as it flashes past the window.
It slows the poem down to a stop.
It shows the speaker is lost.
It makes the poem sound like a letter.
questions.explanation: Each new “Here is” is a new glimpse, so the repetition matches the quick changes of view from a train.

questions.prompt: “Fly as thick as driving rain” (line 6). What does this simile suggest about the sights?
options: They come so fast and so many that they blur together.
It is raining outside the train.
questions.explanation: Driving rain is heavy and fast, so the sights seem to stream past in a blur.

questions.prompt: Put these sights in the order the speaker sees them.
items: a cart running away in the road
questions.explanation: The first stanza lists things in rushing pairs; the second picks out single people and places.

questions.prompt: The poem opens “Faster than fairies, faster than witches”. Why compare the train's speed to fairies and witches?
options: It makes the speed seem magical and thrilling.
It shows the train is evil.
It shows the poem is about a fairy tale.
It makes the train sound slow.
questions.explanation: Fairies and witches are magical, fast-flying figures, so the comparison suggests the ride feels like magic.
questions.misconception: Reading the comparison literally, as if there were real fairies.

questions.prompt: How does Stevenson use sound and pattern to make the train seem fast? Explain 2 features.
questions.model: Stevenson uses a quick, regular beat in lines such as “Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches”, where the pairs joined by and tick past like wheels over rails. He also uses repetition, as each “Here is” in the second stanza is a new sight that is gone almost before it is named, which ends in “Each a glimpse and gone forever!”
checklist: explains 2 features of sound or pattern
supports each with a short quotation
links each feature to the speed of the train
questions.explanation: Say what each sound or pattern does, not just its name.

units.title: Sentences for effect
units.summary: Writers vary sentence length and form to control pace and emphasis. Say why a sentence of that kind is there, at that point.

questions.prompt: How many sentences are there in the extract?
questions.explanation: Count the full stops: the extract has 6 sentences, from “He was beaten” to “aroused.”

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences from the extract is a single-clause sentence?
options: “He was beaten (he knew that); but he was not broken.”
“He had learned the lesson, and in all his after life he never forgot it.”
“It was his introduction to the reign of primitive law, and he met the introduction halfway.”
questions.explanation: It has only one verb (was). Each of the others joins 2 or more clauses.

questions.prompt: Buck saw “once for all” (line 1) that he had no chance against a club. What does once for all mean?
questions.explanation: Once for all means once and for all: he learned the lesson permanently.

questions.prompt: Buck faces the new world “uncowed” (line 5). What does uncowed mean?
questions.explanation: To cow someone is to frighten them into obeying. Un- reverses it.

questions.prompt: Which word joins the 2 main clauses in “He had learned the lesson, and in all his after life he never forgot it.”?
questions.explanation: And is a co-ordinating conjunction joining 2 main clauses, so this is a multi-clause sentence.

questions.prompt: In “It was his introduction to the reign of primitive law, and he met the introduction halfway.” the word introduction is repeated. What is the effect?
options: It links the clauses and shows Buck accepting the new life rather than fighting it.
It shows the writer forgot the word.
It slows the story to a stop.
questions.explanation: Meeting something halfway means accepting it. Repeating the noun ties his response tightly to what has happened to him.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the sentences is true or false.

statements.s: Every sentence in the extract is short.
The extract has 2 sentences that use a semi-colon.
The first sentence contrasts 2 ideas.
The last sentence is a single-clause sentence.

questions.explanation: Sentence lengths vary; semi-colons appear in the first and last sentences; beaten is set against not broken; the last sentence has several clauses.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes: The writer uses a short sentence to make it exciting. Why is this a weak comment?
options: It does not say which sentence or why a short sentence is used at that point.
Short sentences are never used in stories.
It uses the wrong technical term.
questions.explanation: Good comments link the sentence type to the moment, for example a short sentence that sums up the lesson like a blow.
questions.misconception: Labelling a sentence type without explaining why it is used there.

questions.prompt: Why does “but he was not broken” come at the end of the first sentence?
options: Ending on it stresses that his spirit survives, the most important idea.
It is the least important idea.
Sentences must end with a verb.
It explains what a club is.
questions.explanation: The end of a sentence is a position of emphasis, so the contrast lands on not broken.

questions.prompt: How does London use different sentence lengths across the extract to show the change in Buck? Refer to at least 2 sentences.
questions.model: London mixes short and long sentences to mark stages in Buck's change. The very short “That club was a revelation.” stops the reader, just as the lesson stops Buck. After it, the sentences lengthen, and the last one builds through several clauses to the word “aroused”, as if his fierce nature is slowly waking. The pattern moves from defeat to a new, more dangerous strength.
checklist: refers to at least 2 sentences
explains the effect of a short sentence at that point
explains the effect of a long sentence and links it to Buck's change
questions.explanation: Link each sentence length to what is happening to Buck.

units.title: How a text is built: structure
units.summary: Structure is the shape of a whole text. Track how the focus shifts as the text goes on, and say what changes and why it matters.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the story.
items: Maya watches the sea pull back.
She remembers what her grandfather told her.
questions.explanation: The story moves forward in time apart from one short flashback to her grandfather's words.

questions.prompt: Where is the story set?
questions.explanation: Line 1 names “The beach at Saltmarsh Bay”.

questions.prompt: Whose initials are T. O. most likely to be?
questions.explanation: Her grandfather said he “scratched his initials into the boiler”, and Maya finds them on the boiler.

questions.prompt: The paragraph starting on line 4 opens with “Maya stayed.” Why does the writer use such a short sentence here?
options: It contrasts her with everyone who has left and shifts the focus to her.
questions.explanation: Just 2 words after a busy description of people leaving make her decision stand out.

questions.prompt: Line 10 begins “Now the wreck was there”. What does the word Now signal?
options: a return to the present after the flashback
questions.explanation: Lines 7 to 9 look back to her grandfather's story; Now brings us back to the beach.

questions.prompt: What does line 11 add to the structure of the story?
options: a time limit that builds tension
questions.explanation: “She had 40 minutes before the water turned” sets a deadline, so every later action feels urgent.

questions.prompt: Tick the 2 details that are set up early in the story and pay off later.
options: the rocks rising out of the water
the grandfather's initials on the boiler
the sea pulling back further than usual
questions.explanation: The initials are found at the wreck, and the sea that pulled back returns in the last line.

questions.prompt: Which comment about the ending is most precise?
options: The ending makes the reader want to read on.
The last line returns to the sea from the opening, but now it is coming back, so the calm ending hides a threat.
The ending makes the reader feel like they are there.
questions.explanation: It says exactly what links the ending to the start and what effect that creates. The others are vague.
questions.misconception: Using stock phrases about the reader instead of explaining a structural choice.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the structure is true or false.

statements.s: The story covers many years.
Most of the story takes place in about an hour.
The story is told by Maya in the first person.
The focus narrows from the whole beach to a small mark on a boiler.

questions.explanation: The story covers one evening, is told in the third person, and zooms from a wide view to the faint initials.

questions.prompt: How does the writer structure the story to build tension towards the end? Refer to at least 2 structural choices.
questions.model: The writer builds tension by setting a deadline: Maya has “40 minutes before the water turned”, so we watch the clock as she walks out. The pace then quickens as she “started to run”, and the story slows right down at the wreck, where she feels for the initials. The final line, “Behind her, very quietly, the sea began to come back”, leaves her far from shore, so the story ends at its most tense point.
checklist: identifies at least 2 structural choices
supports each with evidence
explains how each builds tension
questions.explanation: Think about the time limit and what the ending leaves unresolved.

units.title: Fact, opinion, viewpoint and bias
units.summary: A fact can be checked; an opinion is a judgement. Bias means presenting only one side, often by exaggerating some points and leaving others out.

questions.prompt: What does the writer want readers to do?
options: tell the council what they think before it decides
questions.explanation: The letter ends “Tell them what you think, before it is too late.”

questions.prompt: Which of these is a fact?
options: “The lights would allow football and netball to be played until 9pm, all year round.”
questions.explanation: The first describes what the plan would do and could be checked. The others are judgements.
questions.misconception: Treating a confident-sounding claim as a fact.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's viewpoint?
questions.explanation: The writer calls the plan “a terrible idea” and urges readers to object.

questions.prompt: “Anyone who has walked there on a winter evening knows how peaceful it is” (lines 3 to 4). How does this try to persuade?
options: It assumes every reader already agrees.
questions.explanation: Saying “Anyone” knows something treats the opinion as if it were common knowledge.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 words that make the floodlights sound unpleasant.
questions.explanation: Glaring, noise and pouring all suggest light and sound that cannot be escaped. Peaceful and quiet describe the park as it is now.

questions.prompt: The letter ends “before it is too late”. What effect does this have?
options: It creates urgency, as if something will soon be lost for ever.
It shows the writer is calm.
It gives a fact about time.
questions.explanation: It pushes readers to act quickly.

questions.prompt: Which group's view does the letter leave out?
options: people who would use the pitch after dark
families who live beside the park
questions.explanation: The writer mentions supporters only briefly and never lets players speak for themselves. Leaving out a side is one form of bias.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the letter is true or false.

statements.s: The writer says how much the sports centres cost to use.
The writer mentions what supporters think.
The writer uses a rhetorical question.
The writer proves the lights would be noisy.

questions.explanation: Line 6 mentions what “Supporters say”; “Why should the families...?” is a rhetorical question. No costs or proof are given.

questions.prompt: The writer calls the park “the last quiet green space in the town” (line 3). Why is the word last effective?
options: It makes the park seem rare and precious, so losing it would be final.
It shows the park is at the edge of town.
It tells us the park is small.
It means the park is the newest.
questions.explanation: Last suggests nothing else like it would remain.

questions.prompt: Explain how the letter is biased. Refer to what the writer includes and what the writer leaves out.
questions.model: The letter is biased because it exaggerates the harm, calling the lights “a glaring car park of noise” and describing light “pouring into their bedrooms every night”. It mentions the supporters' view only to dismiss it with “Of course they do”, and it leaves out the young people who would use the pitch, the possible benefits, and whether the sports centres are affordable or easy to reach.
checklist: identifies exaggeration or loaded language in the letter
explains how the other side is dismissed or left out
uses short quotations as evidence
questions.explanation: Bias is about what is included and what is missing.

units.title: Evaluating a statement about a text
units.summary: To evaluate, weigh the evidence on both sides of a view. Then decide how far you agree and say so clearly.

questions.prompt: What is Mr Utterson's job?
questions.explanation: Line 1 calls him “Mr. Utterson the lawyer”.

questions.prompt: He has a “rugged countenance” (line 1). What does countenance mean?
questions.explanation: Countenance is a formal word for face or expression.

questions.prompt: “He was austere with himself” (line 6). What does austere mean?
questions.explanation: The examples that follow (gin instead of fine wine, no theatre) show him denying himself.

questions.prompt: Tick the 2 pleasures Utterson denies himself.
questions.explanation: He drinks gin “to mortify a taste for vintages” and has not been to the theatre for many years.

questions.prompt: Utterson says “I let my brother go to the devil in his own way.” What does this show about how he treats others?
options: He lets them make their own choices without interfering.
He punishes them for their mistakes.
He has a brother who is a criminal.
He wants them to go to church.
questions.explanation: He does not lecture people who go wrong; he leaves them to their own choices.

questions.prompt: Statement: Utterson judges other people harshly. Which quotation most strongly challenges this?
questions.explanation: Tolerance means accepting others, the opposite of harsh judgement. The other quotations describe how he looks or treats himself.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Utterson talks a great deal at dinner.
His kindness shows most in his actions.
He treats people differently once they get into trouble.
He enjoys the theatre.

questions.explanation: He is “scanty” in discourse; his goodness speaks “in the acts of his life”; he “never marked a shade of change in his demeanour”; he enjoys the theatre though he no longer goes.

questions.prompt: Which sentence moves best from a detail to a bigger idea?
options: Utterson is a lawyer who has a face.
Stevenson suggests that a cold surface can hide real kindness, an idea that matters in a novel about hidden selves.
questions.explanation: Evaluation is strongest when it links details to what the writer seems to be saying about people.
questions.misconception: Staying with details instead of reaching a wider idea.

questions.prompt: Which is the best judgement on the statement: Utterson judges other people harshly?
options: I completely agree, because he never smiles.
I largely disagree: he is strict with himself but tolerant and loyal to others.
I agree, because he is a lawyer.
questions.explanation: This judgement is clear and balanced, and it uses the contrast between how he treats himself and how he treats others.

questions.prompt: How far do you agree that Stevenson presents Utterson as a man who is hard on himself but kind to others? Write a paragraph with a clear judgement.
questions.model: I largely agree. Stevenson shows Utterson is hard on himself: he is “austere with himself” and drinks gin alone to deny himself fine wine. Yet he has “an approved tolerance for others” and is “inclined to help rather than to reprove”, so he is kind to people who go wrong. However, his kindness is quiet rather than warm, since he is “cold, scanty and embarrassed in discourse”, so the kindness shows in actions, not words. Stevenson seems to suggest that a person's dull surface can hide real goodness.
checklist: reaches a clear judgement
supports both parts of the statement with quotations
considers a qualification or the other side
links to a bigger idea about the character
questions.explanation: Decide how far you agree, then weigh the evidence.

units.title: Comparing texts
units.summary: Compare like with like: the same aspect in both texts, with evidence from each, linked by words such as whereas and similarly.

questions.prompt: In Text 1, where is the speaker?
options: on a moving train, looking out
questions.explanation: The title and the sights that “whistle by” show the speaker is riding in a railway carriage.

questions.prompt: In Text 2, what has the station replaced?
questions.explanation: Line 25 says “the Station had swallowed up the playing-field”.

questions.prompt: Dickens says his ticket was collected “like my taxes” (line 20). What attitude does this show?
options: resentment at being made to pay and obey
questions.explanation: Comparing a ticket to taxes suggests something forced on him by officials, which he grumbles about.

questions.prompt: “an ugly dark monster of a tunnel kept its jaws open” (lines 27 to 28). Which technique is this?
options: personification of the tunnel as a hungry beast
questions.explanation: Jaws belong to a living creature, so the tunnel becomes a monster that could swallow more.

questions.prompt: Tick the 2 statements that are true of BOTH texts.
questions.explanation: Stevenson mentions “stringing the daisies” and Dickens mourns the “buttercups and daisies”, but only Stevenson's text is a poem and only his is cheerful.

questions.prompt: Dickens contrasts the old coach, “melodiously called Timpson’s Blue-Eyed Maid”, with the engine “No. 97”. What is the effect?
options: The coach seems friendly and personal; the engine seems cold and machine-like.
questions.explanation: A pretty name against a bare number shows what Dickens feels has been lost.

questions.prompt: Which comparison compares the same aspect of both texts?
options: Stevenson uses rhyme, whereas Dickens is sad.
Stevenson sees the countryside rushing joyfully past, whereas Dickens sees countryside destroyed by the railway.
Stevenson's poem is short, and Dickens mentions taxes.
questions.explanation: Both halves are about the countryside, so the comparison is like for like.
questions.misconception: Comparing one feature of a text with a different feature of the other.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Stevenson's train is fast.
Dickens describes the speed of his train.
Both writers describe parts of nature.
Dickens looks forward to the future, while Stevenson looks back.

questions.explanation: Stevenson is thrilled by speed; Dickens focuses on what the station destroyed and looks back to his childhood.

questions.prompt: Dickens says he had been “defied by Act of Parliament” to object to his luggage label. What is his tone?
questions.explanation: He uses grand legal language about a sticker on a suitcase, which makes fun of railway rules.

questions.prompt: Compare how the 2 writers present the countryside seen from the railway. Use a comparison word and a quotation from each text.
questions.model: Both writers notice the countryside around the railway, but they present it very differently. Stevenson's countryside is full of life and movement: “the horses and cattle” charge past and “here is the green for stringing the daisies”, all glimpsed with delight. In contrast, Dickens's countryside has been destroyed, as the hawthorns, turf and “buttercups and daisies” have given way to “the stoniest of jolting roads”. Stevenson enjoys what the train shows him, whereas Dickens mourns what the railway has taken.
checklist: compares the same aspect (the countryside) in both texts
uses a comparison word such as whereas or in contrast
includes a relevant quotation from each text
explains each writer's attitude
questions.explanation: Keep both texts in every sentence where you can.

units.title: Great Expectations: the churchyard
units.summary: Dickens opens the novel with a small boy alone among his family's graves. The adult Pip narrates, so fear and gentle humour sit side by side.

questions.prompt: Who were “Philip Pirrip, late of this parish, and also Georgiana wife of the above”?
questions.explanation: The narrator is Pip (Philip Pirrip), and he finds his family's names on the gravestones. Late of this parish means they once lived here and have died.

questions.prompt: What is “a great iron on his leg” (line 13)?
options: a heavy ring and chain, showing he is an escaped prisoner
questions.explanation: Prisoners were chained with leg irons. This detail tells the reader the man has escaped.

questions.prompt: What does the phrase “late of this parish” (lines 4 to 5) mean?
options: who used to live here and has now died
who arrived in the parish too late
who lives in the next parish
who is often late for church
questions.explanation: Late here means dead. It is a formal phrase found on gravestones.
questions.misconception: Reading late as meaning not on time.

questions.prompt: What does the man order Pip to do in line 23?
questions.explanation: He says “Show us where you live” and “Pint out the place!”, meaning point out the place.

questions.prompt: Pip says “sir” in almost every reply (lines 18 to 22). What does this suggest?
options: He is terrified and trying to please the man.
He thinks the man is a teacher.
questions.explanation: Repeating sir shows a small boy desperately polite to a frightening stranger, hoping politeness will keep him safe.

questions.prompt: The first paragraph moves from the graves out to the marshes, the river and the sea, then ends with Pip. What is the effect of this structure?
options: The view widens, then shrinks to one tiny, crying boy, so Pip seems small and alone.
It tells us the time of day.
questions.explanation: After the huge, bleak landscape, Pip appears at the very end as “the small bundle of shivers”, which makes him seem helpless.

questions.prompt: The sea is “the distant savage lair from which the wind was rushing” (lines 9 to 10). What does this metaphor suggest?
options: The sea is like a wild beast's den that sends out the wind.
The sea is calm and friendly.
The sea is close to the churchyard.
questions.explanation: A lair belongs to a dangerous animal, so the whole landscape feels threatening, even before the convict appears.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Pip is an adult when these events happen.
The man is wet and muddy.
Pip's village is right next to the church.
The man seizes Pip by the chin.

questions.explanation: Pip is a small child (the adult Pip tells the story later). The man has been “soaked in water, and smothered in mud”. The village is “a mile or more from the church”.

questions.prompt: “I believe they were fat, though I was at that time undersized for my years” (line 27). What does this sentence show about the narrator?
options: He is the grown-up Pip, looking back on his childhood.
He is still a child as he speaks.
He is not sure who he is.
questions.explanation: At that time shows the narrator is older now, remembering. This adult voice adds dry humour to a frightening scene.

questions.prompt: How does Dickens make the churchyard setting frightening before the convict appears? Refer to lines 1 to 10.
questions.model: Dickens makes the setting bleak and threatening. The churchyard is a “bleak place overgrown with nettles”, full of graves, including those of 5 tiny brothers, so death is everywhere. Beyond it lies “the dark flat wilderness” of the marshes and a river described as a “low leaden line”, all dull and lifeless. The wind rushes from a “savage lair”, as if the landscape itself were a beast, and the paragraph ends with Pip beginning to cry, so the reader is already afraid before the man leaps out.
checklist: refers to details from lines 1 to 10
explains the effect of specific words such as bleak, leaden or savage
comments on how the setting prepares for the convict's arrival
questions.explanation: Focus on how individual words build an atmosphere of fear and death.

units.title: A Christmas Carol: meet Scrooge
units.summary: Dickens builds Scrooge through images of cold and through the way other people, and even animals, react to him.

questions.prompt: Scrooge is “a tight-fisted hand at the grind-stone” (line 1). What does tight-fisted mean?
questions.explanation: A tight fist holds on to money and never lets it go.

questions.prompt: Which kind of weather is NOT mentioned in lines 8 to 12?
questions.explanation: Wind, snow, rain, hail and sleet are all mentioned. Fog is not.

questions.prompt: Scrooge speaks in a “grating voice” (line 5). What does grating suggest?
options: harsh and unpleasant, like metal scraping
questions.explanation: A grater scrapes food into pieces, so a grating voice is rough and irritating.

questions.prompt: He is “Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire” (lines 2 to 3). What does this mean?
options: Nobody has ever managed to get any warmth or kindness out of him.
questions.explanation: Flint makes sparks when struck with steel. Saying no spark of generous fire has ever come from him shows he has never been kind.

questions.prompt: Look at lines 13 to 16. Tick the 3 kinds of people who never approach Scrooge.
questions.explanation: Dickens lists beggars, children asking “what it was o’clock”, and people who might inquire “the way to such and such a place”.

questions.prompt: “No warmth could warm, no wintry weather chill him.” What is the effect of the repeated pattern of No?
options: It stresses that nothing at all can affect Scrooge.
It shows Scrooge loves the weather.
It slows the story to a stop.
questions.explanation: The repeated negatives pile up to show that Scrooge is untouched by anything, inside or out.

questions.prompt: Scrooge “iced his office in the dog-days” (line 7). What does this tell you?
options: He kept his office cold even in the hottest days of summer.
He kept dogs in his office.
His office was warm all year.
questions.explanation: Dog-days are the hottest days of summer. Scrooge carries his own cold with him, so his office is chilly whatever the season.

questions.prompt: The rain and snow often “came down” handsomely, “and Scrooge never did.” What is the joke?
options: Came down means fell, and also gave generously; Scrooge never gives anything.
questions.explanation: Dickens plays on 2 meanings of came down: weather falls generously, but Scrooge never comes down with money.
questions.misconception: Missing a pun by reading only one meaning of a phrase.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Scrooge's office is warm in summer.
People greet Scrooge gladly in the street.
Scrooge enjoys keeping people at a distance.
Scrooge's eyes are red and his lips blue.

questions.explanation: He “iced his office in the dog-days”; “Nobody ever stopped him in the street”; keeping sympathy away was “the very thing he liked”; the cold “made his eyes red, his thin lips blue”.

questions.prompt: How does Dickens use humour to present Scrooge? Refer to 2 examples.
questions.model: Dickens uses exaggeration to make Scrooge's meanness funny. Even “the blind men’s dogs appeared to know him” and drag their owners into doorways, which is absurd but shows how completely Scrooge is avoided. He also uses wordplay: the weather often “came down” handsomely, “and Scrooge never did”, a pun on giving money. The humour makes Scrooge entertaining rather than simply hateful, which prepares us to enjoy his later change.
checklist: explains 2 examples of humour
uses short quotations as evidence
says what the humour shows about Scrooge or why Dickens uses it
questions.explanation: Explain how each example is funny and what it reveals about Scrooge.

units.title: Modern fiction: Power Cut
units.summary: Modern stories often use a present-tense, first-person voice and an everyday setting. Look at how small details and dialogue show a change in the narrator.

questions.prompt: At what time do the lights go out?
questions.explanation: Line 1: “At 7.14 the lights go out.”

questions.prompt: Which floor does the narrator's family live on?
questions.explanation: Line 6 says “From the ninth floor I can usually see the whole city”.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
items: The narrator looks out of the window.
Mrs Kowalski knocks with a candle.
Mrs Kowalski tells a story about snow.
The narrator knocks on 9C the next morning.
questions.explanation: The story covers one evening and ends with a short scene the next morning.

questions.prompt: Headlights are “crawling along the ring road like beetles” (line 8). What does the simile suggest?
options: From high up, the cars look tiny and slow.
The road is full of insects.
questions.explanation: From the ninth floor in the dark, moving headlights look small and slow, like insects.
questions.misconception: Reading the simile literally, as if there were insects on the road.

questions.prompt: Mrs Kowalski's face “floats in the gold light like a picture in a locket” (lines 11 to 12). What does this suggest?
options: She seems precious and old-fashioned, like a treasured memory.
questions.explanation: A locket holds a small picture of someone loved. The image makes her seem gentle and special.

questions.prompt: “I’m not frightened,” says Tariq, from under the table. Why is this funny?
options: His hiding place shows he is frightened, which contradicts his words.
Tariq is joking about the table.
Tariq is talking to the cat.
questions.explanation: The action tells the truth that his words deny. The writer shows his fear without saying it.

questions.prompt: “Nobody looks at a screen. There aren’t any to look at.” (line 18) What is the tone of these sentences?
questions.explanation: The first sentence sounds like praise; the second admits they have no choice. The joke hints that the evening without screens turns out to be good.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The story is set in a house in the countryside.
The power is off for more than 2 hours.
Mrs Kowalski brings the candle because she is frightened.
The narrator had talked to Mrs Kowalski many times before.

questions.explanation: It is a tower block, Chandler House, and the power is off from 7.14 to 9.40, more than 2 hours. She brings the candle in case “the little one” is frightened, and the narrator had said only “perhaps 20 words to her”.

questions.prompt: Mrs Kowalski says “That was nice.” The narrator thinks “It was. I don’t say so.” What do these lines suggest?
options: The narrator feels it but is too shy to say it, and shows it by visiting her the next day.
The narrator did not enjoy the evening.
The narrator is angry with Mrs Kowalski.
The narrator did not hear her.
questions.explanation: The narrator's feelings come out in action instead of words, which makes the final gesture more meaningful.

questions.prompt: How does the writer use light and dark in the story? Refer to at least 2 moments.
questions.model: The darkness at the start cuts the family off: the city that is usually “a map drawn in orange dots” has “been rubbed out”, so the narrator feels alone. Into this darkness comes Mrs Kowalski's candle, and her face glows in “the gold light”, so light becomes linked with kindness and company. When the electric lights return they make everyone “squint and laugh”, as if the harsh normal light ends something special, but the narrator carries that warmth into the next morning.
checklist: refers to at least 2 moments involving light or dark
explains what the light or dark represents
links the imagery to the change in the narrator or the characters
questions.explanation: Look at how the writer gives light and dark a meaning beyond the power cut itself.

units.title: Jane Eyre: the red-room
units.summary: Brontë builds a frightening setting from the room's colours and its history. Then she turns Jane's own imagination against her.

questions.prompt: Why is the red-room so rarely slept in (lines 1 to 3)?
options: It is only used when there are so many visitors that every room is needed.
questions.explanation: It is used only when “a chance influx of visitors” means all the space is needed.

questions.prompt: Who died in the red-room?
questions.explanation: Line 19 says “Mr. Reed had been dead nine years: it was in this chamber he breathed his last”.

questions.prompt: Put Jane's actions in order.
items: She sits on a low ottoman by the fireplace.
She gets up to check whether the door is locked.
questions.explanation: Jane hardly moves, which makes the one trip across the room, past the mirror, stand out.

questions.prompt: The bed “stood out like a tabernacle in the centre” (lines 4 to 5). What does this simile suggest?
options: The bed seems sacred and awe-inspiring, like a shrine.
The bed is small and plain.
questions.explanation: A tabernacle is a holy tent or shrine, so the bed seems solemn and almost frightening to approach.

questions.prompt: Jane calls Miss Abbot “bitter” (line 22). What does this word show?
options: Jane sees Miss Abbot as harsh and resentful towards her.
questions.explanation: Bitter suggests resentment and unkindness. We see Miss Abbot through Jane's eyes.
questions.misconception: Taking bitter in its sense of taste rather than as a description of character.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 details that link the room with death.
options: “it was in this chamber he breathed his last”
“hence his coffin was borne by the undertaker’s men”
questions.explanation: The room is where Mr Reed died and lay in his coffin, and it still holds his portrait.

questions.prompt: Jane writes “when I dared move, I got up and went to see” (line 26). What does the word dared show?
options: She is so frightened that even moving feels risky.
She has been told to move.
questions.explanation: Dared suggests courage is needed just to stand up, which shows how afraid she is.

questions.prompt: The mirror repeats “the vacant majesty of the bed and room” (lines 25 to 26). What does vacant majesty suggest?
options: The room is grand but empty, which makes it eerie.
The room is full of people.
The room is small and plain.
questions.explanation: Majesty suggests grandeur, while vacant means empty. The combination makes the room feel hollow and ghostly.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The house-maid cleans the room on Saturdays.
Mrs Reed often sleeps in the room.
The room is silent because it is far from the kitchen.
Jane finds that the door is unlocked.

questions.explanation: The house-maid comes “on Saturdays”; Mrs Reed visits only “at far intervals”; the room is silent “because remote from the nursery and kitchen”; and “no jail was ever more secure”.

questions.prompt: How does Brontë use the history of the room to make it frightening? Refer to the text.
questions.model: Brontë makes the room frightening by filling it with memories of death. Mr Reed “breathed his last” here, “lay in state” here, and his coffin was carried out from here, so the room is linked to every stage of a death. Mrs Reed keeps secrets in a “secret drawer”, including a miniature of her “deceased husband”, which suggests the dead man is still present. Brontë says “a sense of dreary consecration” has kept people away, as if the room were a holy but gloomy tomb, so Jane is locked in a place everyone else avoids.
checklist: refers to Mr Reed's death and what happened in the room
explains words such as consecration, secret or deceased
links the history to Jane's fear or the reader's unease
questions.explanation: Think about why Brontë tells us what happened in the room before Jane looks in the mirror.

units.title: The Speckled Band: Helen's story
units.summary: Detective stories plant clues without explaining them. Look at how strange sounds and changes of pace build suspense in Helen's account.

questions.prompt: Who is telling this part of the story?
questions.explanation: The narrator calls Julia “My sister” and says they “were twins”; Julia calls her “Helen”.

questions.prompt: Why can Helen not sleep that night?
options: She has a vague feeling that something bad is about to happen.
She has drunk too much coffee.
questions.explanation: Line 1: “A vague feeling of impending misfortune impressed me.”

questions.prompt: What does “impending” mean in “impending misfortune” (line 1)?
questions.explanation: Something impending is approaching. The word warns the reader that disaster is near.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 sounds Helen hears that night.
questions.explanation: She hears “the wild scream of a terrified woman”, then “a low whistle” and “a clanging sound”.

questions.prompt: Put these events in order.
items: She hears a whistle and a clang.
Julia falls and cries out about the band.
questions.explanation: Conan Doyle tells the events quickly, one after another, which keeps the tension high.

questions.prompt: Julia's figure is “swaying to and fro like that of a drunkard” (line 11). What does this simile suggest?
options: She has lost control of her body, as if something has poisoned or injured her.
She has been at a party.
questions.explanation: A drunkard cannot walk straight. The comparison suggests that something is badly wrong with Julia's body.

questions.prompt: Julia's door “revolved slowly upon its hinges” (lines 8 to 9). Why is the slow movement effective?
options: It delays what Helen will see, which builds suspense.
It shows the door is new.
questions.explanation: A slowly opening door makes the reader wait, as Helen does, to see what is behind it.

questions.prompt: Helen reminds Holmes how “subtle are the links which bind two souls” (line 2) between twins. Why include this detail?
options: It suggests she sensed the danger, which adds foreboding and makes the loss sharper.
It proves who the killer is.
It shows she dislikes her sister.
questions.explanation: The bond between twins explains her sleepless unease and makes Julia's death more painful.
questions.misconception: Treating every detail in a detective story as a direct clue to the solution.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The stepfather was already at Julia's side when Helen arrived.
Julia recognised Helen before she died.
Medical help from the village saved Julia.
Julia's door was locked when Helen arrived.

questions.explanation: Helen met the stepfather “hastening from his room”; Julia cried out “Helen!”; “all efforts were in vain”; and the door “was unlocked”.

questions.prompt: How does Conan Doyle build tension in Helen's account? Refer to at least 2 methods.
questions.model: Conan Doyle builds tension through a series of strange sounds: the “wild scream”, then “a low whistle” and “a clanging sound”, none of which is explained, so the reader is as puzzled and afraid as Helen. He also controls pace: the door opens “slowly”, making us wait, and then events rush past as Julia falls, writhes and cries out about “The speckled band!” before she can finish. Her unfinished pointing “in the direction of the Doctor’s room” leaves a terrible question hanging.
checklist: identifies at least 2 methods, such as sounds, pace, weather or unfinished clues
supports each with short quotations
explains how each method builds tension
questions.explanation: Explain how each method makes the reader feel uneasy or curious.

units.title: Frankenstein and The War of the Worlds
units.summary: Both writers describe a monstrous creature as it first moves. Compare like with like, such as how each creature looks or how each narrator reacts.

questions.prompt: In Text A, what time is it when the creature opens its eye?
questions.explanation: Line 4: “It was already one in the morning”.

questions.prompt: In Text B, how big does the narrator think the creature is (line 23)?
options: perhaps the size of a bear
questions.explanation: He describes “A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear”.

questions.prompt: How long had Victor worked to make the creature (lines 14 to 15)?
questions.explanation: He had “worked hard for nearly two years”.

questions.prompt: The Martian's mouth has a “lipless brim” (line 26). What is the effect of the word lipless?
options: It makes the creature seem inhuman and unsettling.
It makes the creature seem friendly.
It shows the creature is smiling.
It shows the creature is small.
questions.explanation: A face without lips is not like any human face, so the detail makes the Martian disturbing.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 features Victor had chosen or made to be beautiful.
questions.explanation: He made the limbs in proportion and gave the creature “lustrous black” hair and teeth “of a pearly whiteness”. The eyes and lips are part of the horror.

questions.prompt: Victor ends by trying to find “a few moments of forgetfulness” (lines 20 to 21). What does this show?
options: He wants to escape the horror of what he has done.
He is proud of his work.
He is planning his next experiment.
questions.explanation: He longs to forget, which suggests guilt and horror rather than triumph.

questions.prompt: Wells writes that the mouth “quivered and panted” and the creature “heaved and pulsated convulsively” (lines 27 to 28). What is the effect of these verbs?
options: The creature seems horribly alive and struggling, which disgusts the reader.
The creature seems calm and still.
The creature seems to be singing.
The creature seems to be a machine.
questions.explanation: The verbs describe constant, uncontrolled movement, which makes the creature seem fleshy and repulsive.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Victor had planned the creature's features carefully.
The Martian climbs out quickly.
Both narrators describe the creatures' eyes.
Victor stays in the room to care for the creature.

questions.explanation: Victor had “selected his features as beautiful”; the Martian rises “slowly and painfully”; both describe eyes (“dull yellow eye”, “dark-coloured eyes”); Victor “rushed out of the room”.

questions.prompt: Which sentence compares the same aspect of both texts?
options: Shelley's creature has a “dull yellow eye”, whereas Wells's Martian has “dark-coloured eyes” that stare at the narrator.
Shelley writes about rain, whereas Wells writes about a cylinder.
Text A is longer, and Text B has a glossary.
Victor is a scientist, while the Martian is grey.
questions.explanation: Both halves of the first sentence are about the creatures' eyes, so the comparison is like for like.
questions.misconception: Comparing one feature of a text with a different feature of the other.

questions.prompt: Compare how Shelley and Wells use the creatures' physical appearance to create horror. Refer to both texts.
questions.model: Both writers create horror through close physical detail, but in different ways. Shelley creates horror through contrast: the creature's “lustrous black” hair and “pearly” teeth only form “a more horrid contrast” with its “watery eyes” and “shrivelled complexion”, so beauty makes the ugliness worse. Wells, in contrast, describes something with nothing human about it: a “greyish rounded bulk” that “glistened like wet leather”, with a “lipless” mouth that drops saliva. Shelley's creature is horrifying because it is almost human, whereas Wells's Martian is horrifying because it is completely alien.
checklist: compares physical appearance in both texts
uses quotations from both texts
explains how each writer's details create horror
uses comparison words such as whereas or in contrast
questions.explanation: Keep the comparison on appearance and refer to both texts throughout.

units.title: Pride and Prejudice: the opening
units.summary: Austen's narrator makes a grand statement and then lets the characters' dialogue test it. Irony comes from the gap between what is said and what is meant.

questions.prompt: What news does Mrs Bennet bring?
options: Netherfield Park has been rented at last.
questions.explanation: She asks “have you heard that Netherfield Park is let at last?” Let means rented.

questions.prompt: Who told Mrs Bennet the news?
questions.explanation: Lines 14 to 16: “Mrs. Long has just been here, and she told me all about it.”

questions.prompt: What is the name of the young man who has taken Netherfield?
questions.explanation: Line 34: “Bingley.”

questions.prompt: Put the conversation in order.
items: Mrs Bennet asks if her husband has heard the news.
Mr Bennet says he has not.
Mrs Bennet asks if he wants to know who has taken the house.
She describes the young man and his visit.
They discuss whether he is married.
Mrs Bennet says she is thinking of him marrying one of their daughters.
questions.explanation: Mrs Bennet drives the conversation while Mr Bennet gives her very little.

questions.prompt: How rich is the young man, according to Mrs Bennet?
questions.explanation: She says he has “four or five thousand a year”, a very large income at the time.

questions.prompt: “Mr. Bennet made no answer.” (line 17) What does his silence suggest?
options: He is teasing his wife by refusing to show interest.
He is angry with Mrs Long.
questions.explanation: His later reply shows he knows she is desperate to tell him, so his silence is deliberate teasing.

questions.prompt: After Mr Bennet's reply, the narrator says “This was invitation enough.” (line 22) What does this suggest about Mrs Bennet?
options: The smallest encouragement is enough to set her talking.
She has been invited to a ball.
questions.explanation: Mr Bennet's reply is hardly an invitation, so the narrator gently mocks how eager she is to gossip.

questions.prompt: A single rich man is considered “the rightful property” (line 8) of a neighbour's daughter. What is ironic about this phrase?
options: It reverses who owns whom: the rich man is treated as something the families can claim.
It shows the man owns a lot of property.
It means the house belongs to the daughters.
There is nothing ironic about it.
questions.explanation: In the period a wife's property passed to her husband, so calling the man the families' property turns the usual idea upside down.
questions.misconception: Missing irony by taking the narrator's words at face value.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The young man came to see the house on a Monday.
He will move in after Michaelmas.
Mrs Bennet hopes he will marry one of her daughters.
He comes from the south of England.

questions.explanation: He “came down on Monday”; he takes possession “before Michaelmas”; Mrs Bennet is “thinking of his marrying one of them”; he is “from the north of England”.

questions.prompt: How does the conversation between Mr and Mrs Bennet test the “truth” stated in the opening sentence? Refer to the text.
questions.model: The opening sentence claims that a rich single man “must be in want of a wife”, which sounds like a universal truth. The conversation shows that the want really belongs to Mrs Bennet: she knows nothing of Bingley's feelings, but within moments of hearing of a “man of large fortune” she is “thinking of his marrying one of them”. Mr Bennet's dry question, “how can it affect them?”, pretends not to understand, which exposes her scheming. The dialogue turns the grand opening into a joke about mothers hunting rich husbands for their daughters.
checklist: explains what the opening sentence claims
uses Mrs Bennet's words to show whose wish it really is
comments on Mr Bennet's role or the irony
reaches a view on how the conversation mocks or proves the statement
questions.explanation: Look at how Austen sets the narrator's statement against what the characters actually say.

units.title: To Build a Fire: into the cold
units.summary: London's narrator tells us more than the man understands about the danger. Setting and character together hint at what will happen.

questions.prompt: What time is it when the man looks at his watch?
questions.explanation: Line 4: “It was nine o’clock.” Day had already broken, so it is morning.

questions.prompt: In which direction does the little-travelled trail lead?
questions.explanation: Lines 2 to 3: a “dim and little-travelled trail led eastward”.

questions.prompt: Why does the man pause at the top of the bank?
questions.explanation: Line 3: “he paused for breath at the top”.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 things the man would use to guard against the frost (lines 16 to 17).
questions.explanation: London lists “mittens, ear-flaps, warm moccasins, and thick socks”.

questions.prompt: He excuses his stop “to himself by looking at his watch” (line 4). What does this suggest about him?
options: He does not like to admit he is tired or weak.
He is late for a meeting.
He is afraid of the dark.
questions.explanation: Looking at his watch gives him a reason to stop that is not tiredness, which hints at pride.

questions.prompt: The man does not think about his “frailty as a creature of temperature” (line 13). What does this phrase mean?
options: Humans can only survive within a narrow range of heat and cold.
questions.explanation: The next words explain it: man is “able only to live within certain narrow limits of heat and cold”.

questions.prompt: The sun “would just peep above the sky-line and dip immediately from view” (line 9). What does this personification suggest?
options: The sun is weak and shy, offering only a brief, useless moment of light.
The sun is strong and warm.
The sun is setting for ever.
questions.explanation: Peep and dip make the sun seem timid, so there is no real warmth or comfort to be had.

questions.prompt: “This fact did not worry the man.” (line 7) How does this short sentence create unease?
options: The narrator hints that the man should be worried, so the reader worries instead.
It shows the man is wise.
It shows the weather is improving.
questions.explanation: The narrator knows more than the man. A calm statement about not worrying makes the reader sense danger he is ignoring.
questions.misconception: Assuming that because the character is not worried, the reader should not be either.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: There are clouds in the sky.
The man has not seen the sun for days.
The man thinks deeply about what the cold means.
It is a clear day.

questions.explanation: There is “not a cloud in the sky” and “It was a clear day”; it “had been days since he had seen the sun”; the facts do not “lead him to meditate”.

questions.prompt: What is the narrator's attitude towards the man? Use evidence to support your view.
questions.model: The narrator seems critical of the man, even a little scornful. He says plainly that “The trouble with him was that he was without imagination”, and that he understood “the things of life, but only in the things, and not in the significances”. The repeated phrase “Fifty degrees below zero” mocks his flat thinking, since to him it was “just precisely fifty degrees below zero” and nothing more. Yet the narrator also seems to pity him, as he is a fragile “creature of temperature” who does not see the danger he is walking into.
checklist: states a clear view of the narrator's attitude
supports it with short quotations
explains how the narrator's words reveal that attitude
considers more than one feeling, such as criticism and pity
questions.explanation: Look at the words the narrator chooses when judging the man.

units.title: The Story-Teller: a complete short story
units.summary: Saki tells a story inside a story. Watch how the children react to each story-teller, and how the twist mocks stories with neat moral lessons.

questions.prompt: What is the next stop for the train?
questions.explanation: Lines 2 to 3: “the next stop was at Templecombe, nearly an hour ahead”.

questions.prompt: What colour is the wolf in the bachelor's story?
questions.explanation: The bachelor says it was “Mud-colour all over, with a black tongue and pale grey eyes”.

questions.prompt: What does the smaller girl keep reciting?
options: the first line of a poem
questions.explanation: She recites “On the Road to Mandalay” but “only knew the first line”.

questions.prompt: The aunt and children are like “a housefly that refuses to be discouraged” (lines 13 to 14). What does this simile suggest?
options: Their talk is persistent and annoying.
They are about to fly away.
questions.explanation: A housefly keeps buzzing back however often you wave it away, just like their endless chatter.
questions.misconception: Reading the simile literally.

questions.prompt: Put these events of Bertha's story in order.
items: She is allowed to walk in the Prince's park.
She finds there are no flowers.
A wolf comes into the park.
She hides in the myrtle bushes.
questions.explanation: The bachelor sets up the medals early, and they cause her death at the end.

questions.prompt: Why are there no sheep in the Prince's park (lines 149 to 154)?
options: His mother dreamed he would be killed by a sheep or a clock.
questions.explanation: The bachelor invents a ridiculous reason that the children accept at once.

questions.prompt: “The aunt suppressed a gasp of admiration.” (line 155) What does this show?
options: Even the aunt is impressed by his clever answer, though she does not want to show it.
The aunt is frightened of sheep.
questions.explanation: Suppressed means held back: she admires his quick invention but will not admit it.

questions.prompt: The aunt says “You have undermined the effect of years of careful teaching.” What does she mean?
options: His story has taught the opposite of the moral lessons she has been teaching.
He has taught the children to read.
He has been a good teacher.
questions.explanation: Her stories teach that goodness is rewarded; his shows a good girl being eaten because of her medals.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The bachelor tells a story because the aunt challenges him.
Bertha hides among myrtle bushes.
The wolf finds Bertha by her smell.
The bachelor gets off the train at Templecombe.

questions.explanation: The aunt says “Perhaps you would like to tell them a story”. The myrtle's scent hides Bertha, but the wolf hears her medals clinking. The bachelor walks “down the platform of Templecombe station”.

questions.prompt: How does Saki present the bachelor? Is he kind, mischievous or both? Give your view with evidence.
questions.model: Saki presents the bachelor as mischievous more than kind. At first he seems unfriendly: the aunt decides he is “a hard, unsympathetic man”.
