questions.prompt: “I am not that man.” (line 6) What does Douglass mean?
options: He is not someone who would refuse to celebrate real freedom.
He is not grateful to anyone.
questions.explanation: After the questions about who would refuse to rejoice, he says he would gladly celebrate if freedom were truly shared.

questions.prompt: Douglass speaks of “the immeasurable distance between us” (line 10). What does he mean?
options: There is a vast gap between his free audience and enslaved people like him.
He lives far away from the audience.
He is standing far from the stage.
He has travelled a long way.
questions.explanation: The distance is not in miles but in rights and freedom.

questions.prompt: The “lame man leap as an hart” (line 7) is a phrase from the Bible. What does it suggest?
questions.explanation: A lame man leaping like a deer is a picture of impossible happiness, which is how freedom would feel.

questions.prompt: “You may rejoice, I must mourn.” (lines 13 to 14) Which technique is used?
options: antithesis, setting opposites side by side
questions.explanation: Rejoice and mourn, you and I, may and must are balanced against each other to show the division.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 blessings Douglass says the audience has inherited (line 11).
questions.explanation: He lists “justice, liberty, prosperity, and independence”, inherited by the audience but not by him.

questions.prompt: “The sunlight that brought life and healing to you, has brought stripes and death to me.” (lines 12 to 13) What does this metaphor suggest?
options: The same event brought freedom to some and suffering to others.
questions.explanation: Sunlight usually means good things, so showing it bring stripes and death exposes the injustice.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Douglass says he is included in the celebration.
He calls asking him to join the celebration a kind of mockery.
He addresses the audience as citizens.
He thanks the audience for their kindness.

questions.explanation: He says “I am not included”; he calls it “inhuman mockery”; he asks “Do you mean, citizens, to mock me”; he does not thank them.

questions.prompt: Douglass calls the celebration “sacrilegious irony” (line 15). What does he mean?
options: It disrespects something sacred, because liberty is celebrated while people are enslaved.
It is a mistake in the programme.
questions.explanation: Sacrilegious means disrespecting something holy. Celebrating liberty while denying it to others insults the ideal itself.
questions.misconception: Thinking irony always means something is funny.

questions.prompt: How does Douglass use contrast to challenge his audience? Refer to at least 2 examples.
questions.model: Douglass builds his speech on contrasts between “you” and “me”. The blessings of liberty are “shared by you, not by me”, and “This Fourth of July is yours, not mine”, so the audience cannot avoid seeing the division. He contrasts the sunlight that brought “life and healing” with “stripes and death”, making the same event mean freedom for some and suffering for others. The antithesis “You may rejoice, I must mourn” forces the free audience to see their celebration through the eyes of the enslaved, which turns a festival into a challenge.
checklist: explains at least 2 contrasts
supports each with short quotations
explains how each contrast challenges the audience
questions.explanation: Notice how often Douglass sets you against me.

units.title: Letters and travel writing: Isabella Bird
units.summary: Bird writes to her sister about a dangerous climb. Vivid verbs and her personal opinions bring the experience to life for a reader far away.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the narrow passage between 2 rocks (line 3)?
questions.explanation: They squeezed through a passage called the “Dog’s Lift” at the top of the gorge.

questions.prompt: How did Bird get through the passage (lines 3 to 4)?
options: She climbed on a man's shoulders and was hauled up.
She crawled through on her hands and knees.
questions.explanation: She “climbed on the shoulders of one man and then was hauled up”.

questions.prompt: For how many feet does the Peak look nearly vertical (lines 6 to 7)?
questions.explanation: Lines 6 to 7: the Peak “looks nearly vertical for 400 feet”.

questions.prompt: The climbers have “throbbing hearts and panting lungs” (lines 1 to 2). What do these details show?
options: The climb is exhausting in the thin mountain air.
The climbers are excited about lunch.
The climbers are ill with a fever.
questions.explanation: The physical details make the reader feel the effort of climbing at altitude.

questions.prompt: What happened to Ring, the dog (lines 11 to 12)?
options: He refused to cross the Ledge and stayed behind howling.
He ran ahead to the top.
questions.explanation: Bird writes that Ring “refused to traverse the Ledge” and stayed behind at the Lift, “howling piteously”.

questions.prompt: Most climbers think the shelf is the most dangerous part, but “it does not seem so to me” (lines 8 to 9). What does this show about Bird?
options: She is confident and gives her own honest judgement.
She is trying to frighten her sister.
questions.explanation: She explains her reasons (secure foothold, something to hold), which shows a thoughtful, confident traveller.

questions.prompt: Bird writes “to my thinking, the worst part of the climb” (line 10). What does the phrase to my thinking add?
options: It shows a personal opinion, as you would share with a close reader in a letter.
It is a fact about the mountain.
It shows she is unsure what she thinks.
questions.explanation: Personal phrases like this give the letter a friendly, confiding voice.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Bird climbs alone.
The shelf is usually considered the most dangerous part of the climb.
Bird agrees that the shelf is the most dangerous part.
The dog crossed the Ledge.

questions.explanation: She is with others (“we reached the top”); the shelf “is usually considered the most dangerous part”, though “it does not seem so to me”; Ring “refused to traverse the Ledge”.

questions.prompt: Bird imagines a fall leaving “a shapeless, bloody heap” (line 11). Why might she include such a shocking image in a letter to her sister?
options: to make her sister feel the real danger and the thrill she felt
to frighten her sister into staying at home
questions.explanation: The graphic image makes the height real for a reader who was not there.
questions.misconception: Assuming the writer is describing something that actually happened rather than imagining it.

questions.prompt: How does Bird make the climb vivid for her reader? Refer to at least 2 methods.
questions.model: Bird throws the reader straight into the effort with the verbs “Slipping, faltering, gasping”, which sound breathless and continuous. She gives precise details of the danger, such as a Peak “nearly vertical for 400 feet” and “the most tremendous precipice I have ever seen”, so her sister can picture the scale. Her personal comments, such as “to my thinking, the worst part of the climb”, make it feel as if she is talking directly to her reader.
checklist: explains at least 2 methods, such as verbs, precise details, imagery or personal voice
supports each with short quotations
links each method to how it helps a distant reader imagine the climb
questions.explanation: Remember that the reader is her sister, far away in Britain.

units.title: Literary non-fiction: Dickens's Night Walks
units.summary: Dickens turns his sleepless walks into an essay full of humour and sympathy, personifying London as a restless sleeper.

questions.prompt: Why did Dickens walk the streets at night?
options: He worked as a night watchman.
He was looking for a lost friend.
questions.explanation: Line 1 mentions “a temporary inability to sleep”.

questions.prompt: In which month did the walks take place?
questions.explanation: Line 8: “The month was March”.

questions.prompt: His walks brought him into “sympathetic relations” (line 6) with homeless people. What does this mean?
options: He came to share and understand their feelings.
questions.explanation: Sympathetic here means feeling with someone. Walking all night helped him understand people with nowhere to go.

questions.prompt: At what time did Dickens usually set out?
questions.explanation: Line 9 says “half-past twelve” was “about my time for confronting it”.

questions.prompt: He calls his experience “a fair amateur experience of houselessness” (line 5). What is the effect of amateur?
options: It admits he is only trying it out and is not truly homeless, which is modest and slightly ironic.
It shows he is an expert.
questions.explanation: An amateur is not a professional. Dickens could go home at sunrise, unlike the people he meets.

questions.prompt: Dickens writes “Houselessness even observed” (line 20), with a capital letter. What is the effect?
options: Houselessness becomes like a character watching the city, standing for all the homeless walkers.
It is the name of a street.
It shows the start of a new sentence.
questions.explanation: Giving the word a capital turns a condition into a figure who notices things.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 places Dickens names where the peace was sometimes broken (lines 16 to 18).
questions.explanation: He names “the Haymarket”, “Kent-street in the Borough” and “the Old Kent-road”. Oxford Street appears only in the modern article.

questions.prompt: Dickens describes “the thin-armed, puff-faced, leaden-lipped gin-drinker” (line 24). What is the effect of these compound adjectives?
options: They sketch the person quickly and vividly, with a mix of humour and pity.
They make the person seem healthy.
They slow the passage down to a stop.
questions.explanation: Each hyphenated adjective adds a sharp detail, building a picture like a cartoon.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Dickens was cured by staying in bed.
When the pubs closed, some of the night's company was lost.
Fights broke out often.
London is compared to a citizen with fits of restlessness.

questions.explanation: He was cured by “getting up directly after lying down”; company was lost when “the late public-houses turned their lamps out”; there was “surprisingly little” fighting; London acts “as if in imitation of individual citizens”.
questions.misconception: Taking Dickens's joke about being lucky to see a fight as a statement that fights were common.

questions.prompt: What is Dickens's attitude to the people he meets at night? Support your view with evidence.
questions.model: Dickens's attitude is a mixture of amused detachment and real sympathy. He jokes about drunk people being “magnetically attracted towards each other” and meeting “to fraternise or fight”, which treats them almost like a scientific curiosity. Yet he says his walks brought him into “sympathetic relations” with people who have “no other object every night in the year”, and he notices sad details such as the gin-drinker “dressed in soiled mourning”. Overall he laughs at the night's oddities but does not look down on the people living through them.
checklist: states a clear view of Dickens's attitude
considers both humour and sympathy
supports the view with short quotations
explains how the language reveals the attitude
questions.explanation: Weigh his humour against his sympathy before you decide.

units.title: A modern article: London after dark
units.summary: Articles use a headline, standfirst, subheadings and quotations to guide readers. Look at how the organisation and the details present the night city.

questions.prompt: What is the headline of the article?
questions.explanation: The headline is the main title, in line 2. Line 1 is a label showing the section of the publication.

questions.prompt: Which night bus route does the article mention?
questions.explanation: Line 6 mentions “the number 25 night bus”.

questions.prompt: How long has the driver done this route?
questions.explanation: Line 7: he “has done this route for 9 years”.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 kinds of night worker the article mentions.
questions.explanation: Line 6 lists “cleaners”, “bakers” and “a nurse who has just finished a 12-hour shift”.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of the article in order.
items: an opening paragraph about day and night
the section about a quieter city
questions.explanation: The article moves through the night in time order, from midnight to the morning commute.

questions.prompt: The first paragraph contrasts London by day with what happens “between midnight and dawn”. Why open this way?
options: It starts from what readers know, then sets up the surprising idea of a second city.
It shows the writer prefers the day.
It tells readers how to get to London.
questions.explanation: Readers know the daytime crowds; the article then promises to show them something new.

questions.prompt: “the air smells of wet stone instead of exhaust” (line 10). What does this sensory detail suggest?
options: The city is fresh and quiet, without the usual traffic.
questions.explanation: Replacing traffic fumes with the smell of freshly washed pavements shows how different the city feels at night.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the article is true or false.

statements.s: The article is written in the past tense throughout.
The people in it are real.
The article ends in the morning.
The driver says the night bus is mostly parties.

questions.explanation: It uses the present tense; the source line says the people are invented; it ends with “Morning”; the driver says it is “mostly people who keep the city running”.
questions.misconception: Assuming that a quotation in an article must come from a real person.

questions.prompt: The commuters appear “with no idea of the night that has just ended beneath their feet” (line 12). What is the effect of ending this way?
options: The reader now knows a secret the commuters do not, which gives the ending a quiet irony.
It shows the commuters are rude.
It asks the reader a question.
questions.explanation: Having read the article, we know about the hidden night city that the daytime crowds never notice.
questions.misconception: Reading beneath their feet literally, as if something were happening underground.

questions.prompt: How does the writer present the night workers positively? Refer to at least 2 details.
questions.model: The writer presents the night workers as the people the whole city quietly depends on. The article lists real jobs, “cleaners heading for empty office blocks, bakers starting before the sun”, and a nurse at the end of “a 12-hour shift”, which shows how hard they work. The driver's words, “It’s mostly people who keep the city running while everyone else is in bed”, suggest the rest of London depends on them, and repeating them as a pull quote makes this the main idea. The writer also corrects the belief that “the night bus is all parties”, so readers see the workers with new respect.
checklist: refers to at least 2 details about the workers
explains how the details create a positive impression
comments on the use of the quotation or pull quote
questions.explanation: Look at which details the writer chooses and why.

units.title: Comparing viewpoints across time
units.summary: Compare like with like: what each writer notices about London at night, the mood, the attitude and the methods, and think about when each text was written.

questions.prompt: When was Text 1 first published as a book?
questions.explanation: The heading to Text 1 gives the date, 1861.

questions.prompt: Which text describes the writer's own experience using I?
questions.explanation: Dickens writes “caused me to walk about the streets”. The article reports on other people.

questions.prompt: Both texts imagine London trying to sleep. Which statement compares them accurately?
options: Dickens's London “tumbles and tosses before it can get to sleep”, whereas the modern capital “does not sleep” at all but “changes shift”.
Both writers say London sleeps soundly.
Dickens says London never sleeps, whereas the article says it sleeps all night.
questions.explanation: Both writers personify the city, but Dickens shows a restless sleeper while the article shows a city that keeps working.

questions.prompt: How do the forms of the 2 texts differ?
options: Text 1 is a continuous personal essay; Text 2 is an article with a headline, standfirst and subheadings.
Text 1 has subheadings; Text 2 has none.
questions.explanation: The article's organisational features help a modern reader skim, while Dickens's essay flows as one long reflection.

questions.prompt: Tick the 2 statements that are true of both texts.
options: Both describe people who are out at night.
Both name a particular London street.
questions.explanation: Dickens names the Haymarket and the Old Kent-road, and the article names Oxford Street. Only Dickens describes drunkards; only the article has a fox.

questions.prompt: Which feature of Text 2 shows it is written for modern readers who may skim?
options: the subheadings and the pull quote
questions.explanation: Subheadings and a pull quote let a reader grasp the main points at a glance.

questions.prompt: Dickens writes “fifty to one but that specimen was dressed in soiled mourning”. What is the tone of this betting phrase?
options: wry and humorous, though the detail is sad
questions.explanation: He uses the language of a bet to describe a sad sight, which is typical of his mix of humour and pity.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Both writers describe London in March.
Both writers present a London that most readers never see.
Text 2 includes a quotation from a person at work.
Dickens describes workers keeping the city running.

questions.explanation: Only Dickens names the month. Both reveal a hidden night city. The article quotes the bus driver; Dickens focuses on the homeless and the drunk.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is like for like?
options: Dickens's night people are mostly homeless or drunk, whereas the modern night people are mostly workers.
Dickens uses long sentences, whereas the article mentions a fox.
Dickens wrote in 1861, and the article has a headline.
Dickens is funny, while the article has subheadings.
questions.explanation: Both halves of the comparison are about the people who are out at night.
questions.misconception: Comparing one aspect of a text with a different aspect of the other.

questions.prompt: Compare how the 2 writers present quietness and noise in London at night. Refer to both texts.
questions.model: Both writers show a city that grows quieter as the night goes on, but they hear it differently. Dickens's London is restless: it “tumbles and tosses before it can get to sleep”, and even after the pubs close, “if one cab rattled by, half-a-dozen would surely follow”, so the quiet keeps breaking. In contrast, the modern writer presents a calm that feels peaceful: “By 4am the traffic lights change for nobody” and a fox wanders Oxford Street undisturbed. Dickens, writing about the Victorian city he walked through, finds the night uneasy and broken, whereas the modern article finds a gentle, almost magical stillness in the early hours.
checklist: compares quietness and noise in both texts
uses quotations from both texts
uses comparison words such as whereas or in contrast
refers to when each text was written
questions.explanation: Keep both texts in view and compare the same aspect throughout.

units.title: Planning and paragraphing
units.summary: Give each paragraph one clear idea, open it with a topic sentence, and link it to the paragraph before so the whole piece flows.

questions.prompt: What is a topic sentence?
options: the sentence that opens a paragraph and tells the reader what it is about
the last sentence of a story
a sentence that asks a question
a sentence with a quotation in it
questions.explanation: A topic sentence sets the focus. The rest of the paragraph develops it.

questions.prompt: Tick the 4 good reasons to start a new paragraph.
questions.explanation: Paragraphs follow changes in idea, time, place or speaker, not a fixed number of sentences.
questions.misconception: Thinking paragraphs should be a set length rather than following changes in the writing.

questions.prompt: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of school trips to museums?
options: Museum trips let pupils see real objects that bring their lessons to life.
Last year we went on a coach.
questions.explanation: It states one clear idea that the rest of the paragraph can develop with examples.

questions.prompt: Which sentence would be the best link at the start of a paragraph giving the opposite view?
options: On the other hand, some people worry about the cost.
Also, the skate park is good.
questions.explanation: On the other hand signals a change of direction, so the reader expects the counter-argument.

questions.prompt: Put these topic sentences in the best order for an article titled Should our town build a skate park?
items: Our town has nowhere for teenagers to skate safely.
A skate park would give young people a place to meet and keep active.
Some residents fear the noise it might bring.
With careful planning, the benefits would outweigh the worries.
questions.explanation: The order moves from the problem, to the benefits, to the counter-argument, to a balanced conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which sentence does NOT belong in a paragraph about why the school needs more water fountains?
options: My cousin has a new puppy.
Pupils queue for several minutes at the only fountain.
Many pupils feel thirsty after PE.
Bottles can only be refilled at lunchtime.
questions.explanation: The puppy has nothing to do with the paragraph's topic, so it breaks the focus.
questions.misconception: Including any sentence that comes to mind instead of keeping to the paragraph's one idea.

questions.prompt:
Complete the link with a suitable adverbial.
The footpath had been closed for months. ___, the council agreed to repair it.
questions.explanation: An adverbial that shows time or result links the 2 sentences smoothly.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about planning is true or false.

statements.s: A quick plan helps you put ideas in a sensible order.
Every paragraph should cover as many ideas as possible.
Reading only your topic sentences should give the outline of the whole piece.
Linking words are only needed in the last paragraph.

questions.explanation: Plans and topic sentences give a clear structure, and links are needed between every pair of paragraphs.

questions.prompt: Which opening sentence links best to a paragraph that ended: ...and so the canteen now throws away fewer cups.
options: Fewer cups is a good start, but the canteen still wastes a lot of food.
Football is popular at our school.
questions.explanation: It picks up the last idea (fewer cups) and moves the reader on to the next one (food waste).

questions.prompt: Write one paragraph for an article called Why everyone should learn to swim. Include a topic sentence, develop it with 2 examples, and end with a sentence that links to a next paragraph about cost.
questions.model: Learning to swim is one of the most useful skills a person can have. It could save your life if you fell into a river or the sea, and it lets you join in with holidays, sports and days out with friends. Swimming is also a form of exercise that people of almost any age can enjoy. Of course, all of this depends on lessons being affordable, which is not always the case.
checklist: opens with a clear topic sentence
develops the idea with 2 examples
keeps to one focus throughout
ends with a sentence that links to the next paragraph
questions.explanation: Check that every sentence supports the topic sentence.

units.title: Openings that work
units.summary: A strong opening sets up the voice and setting and raises a question in the reader's mind. You do not need to explain everything at once.

questions.prompt: Which opening starts in the middle of the action?
options: The ladder slipped, and Ellis grabbed the gutter with both hands.
My name is Ellis and I am 13.
This is a story about a ladder.
Once upon a time there was a boy.
questions.explanation: It drops the reader straight into a tense moment.

questions.prompt: Match each opening to the technique it uses.
pairs: The whole village knew the clock had stopped.
Fog lay on the canal like grey wool.
Hamza vaulted the fence and kept running.
questions.explanation: Each technique hooks the reader in a different way.

questions.prompt: Which opening raises the strongest question in the reader's mind?
options: Nobody had used the back stairs since the night of the fire.
I woke up and had breakfast.
questions.explanation: The reader wants to know what happened on the night of the fire and why the stairs are avoided.

questions.prompt:
Why is this a weak opening?
Hi, my name is Grace and this story is about the scariest day of my life.
options: It tells the reader everything instead of showing a moment, so there is nothing to discover.
questions.explanation: Announcing what the story is about removes the mystery. Starting inside the scary moment works better.
questions.misconception: Believing that a story should begin by introducing the narrator and summarising the plot.

questions.prompt: Which opening creates the clearest narrative voice?
options: I have never trusted pigeons, and after Tuesday I never will.
Pigeons are birds that live in towns.
questions.explanation: The narrator's opinion and humour come through at once, so we hear a distinct person.

questions.prompt: Which opening is built on a single detail of setting?
options: A single red glove lay on the frozen pond.
Mum said we were moving house.
Everyone in our street has a secret.
questions.explanation: It focuses on one precise image, which makes the reader wonder whose glove it is.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about openings is true or false.

statements.s: An opening should explain all the background straight away.
Starting with dialogue can create instant tension.
A striking statement can make the reader want to find out more.
Every story should begin with the narrator waking up.

questions.explanation: Good openings hold back information. Waking-up openings are common and rarely interesting.

questions.prompt:
Which revision best improves this opening?
It was a dark and stormy night and I was scared.
options: Rain hammered the skylight, and every time the lightning flashed I saw the empty rocking chair move.
It was a very dark and very stormy night and I was very scared.
It was night. It was dark. It was stormy.
I was scared because it was a dark and stormy night.
questions.explanation: It shows the fear through precise details instead of stating it with a well-worn phrase.

questions.prompt: Why might a writer choose to open with a single detail of setting rather than action?
options: to create a mood and make the reader curious before anything happens
because action is not allowed in openings
questions.explanation: A carefully chosen detail can set the atmosphere and plant a question.

questions.prompt: Write an opening of 3 or 4 sentences for a story called The Last Train. Start in the middle of the action and leave the reader with a question.
questions.model: The doors were already sliding shut when Niamh threw herself through the gap. Breathless, she slumped into the nearest seat before she realised the carriage was completely empty. No passengers, no guard, and on every seat lay a single white envelope with her name on it.
checklist: begins in the middle of the action
creates a clear setting with precise details
leaves the reader with a question
uses accurate, varied sentences
questions.explanation: Hold back the explanation so that the reader wants to keep going.

units.title: Narrative: one moment, not a whole life
units.summary: Strong short stories focus on one moment of change. Slow that moment down, and show how the character is different afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which story idea focuses on a single moment?
options: the 30 seconds before Kwame steps onto the stage for his first solo
Kwame's whole life from birth to old age
questions.explanation: A short moment can be explored in detail, so the story feels vivid instead of rushed.

questions.prompt: What is a recount?
options: a list of events joined by and then, with little detail or feeling
a story told in the present tense
questions.explanation: Recounts move from event to event without slowing down, so nothing feels important.
questions.misconception: Thinking that more events make a better story.

questions.prompt: Which sentence slows down a key moment?
options: Her hand hovered over the handle; the metal was cold, and somewhere inside a floorboard creaked.
She opened the door and went in.
questions.explanation: Small sensory details stretch out the moment and build tension.

questions.prompt: Tick the 2 endings that are usually best avoided.
options: She folded the letter and, for the first time, smiled.
The sea began to come back, very quietly.
questions.explanation: Dream endings cancel everything that happened, which feels like a trick to the reader.

questions.prompt: Which ending best shows that a character has changed?
options: The next morning, Rhys knocked on his neighbour's door to say sorry.
Rhys was a different person now, he thought.
questions.explanation: An action shows the change instead of telling it.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a short story plan in a sensible order.
items: a hook that drops the reader into the scene
an ending that echoes the opening
questions.explanation: Most of the words should go on the key moment.

questions.prompt: Which detail best shows that a character is nervous, without saying so?
options: Zara picked at the edge of her ticket until it tore.
questions.explanation: A small action lets the reader work out the feeling.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about short stories is true or false.

statements.s: A short story can take place in less than an hour.
Talking animals always make a story stronger.
Holding back some details can build suspense.
Every event in the character's day should be included.

questions.explanation: Focus and selection make short stories powerful.

questions.prompt: Bilal's 200-word story covers 5 years. What is the best advice for improving it?
options: Choose the single most important moment and expand it with detail.
questions.explanation: Covering years in 200 words forces a list of events. One moment can be explored properly.

questions.prompt: Write the key moment (about 120 words) of a story in which a character waits for a phone call that will change everything. Slow the moment down with detail.
questions.model: The phone lay face down on the kitchen table. Leah had turned it over twice already, as if that might make it ring. The clock above the cooker ticked past 4. She refilled the kettle she had boiled 10 minutes ago and forgot to switch it on. Outside, a bus sighed at the stop and pulled away. When the buzz finally came, it rattled the phone against the wood so loudly that she jumped. For a second she couldn't move. Then she turned it over, read the name on the screen, and pressed the green button with a finger that would not keep still.
checklist: focuses on one moment
slows the moment down with sensory detail
shows the character's feelings through actions
uses varied, accurate sentences
questions.explanation: Stay inside the moment rather than jumping ahead to what happens next.

units.title: Descriptive writing: zoom in, don't tour
units.summary: Pick a few details and develop each one instead of walking round a scene listing everything. Use precise words and the senses to create a mood.

questions.prompt: Which description zooms in rather than touring?
options: One stall sold only lemons, piled into a yellow pyramid that glowed under the striped awning.
On my left there was a stall. On my right there was another stall. In front there was a stall.
There were lots of stalls with lots of things.
questions.explanation: It develops one detail fully, which creates a vivid picture.

questions.prompt:
Which verb is the most precise?
The old man ___ along the icy path.
questions.explanation: Shuffled shows how he moves: slowly and carefully, with small steps.

questions.prompt: Match each sense to the sentence about a seaside town.
pairs: Gulls wheeled above the striped beach huts.
The pier's boards creaked under every footstep.
Salt and hot vinegar drifted from the chip shop.
Wet sand clung to the backs of her legs.
questions.explanation: Using different senses builds a fuller picture than sight alone.

questions.prompt: Which word best suits the mood of a quiet library late in the afternoon?
questions.explanation: Hushed fits the quiet mood. The other words are showy and do not match the scene.
questions.misconception: Using impressive-sounding words that do not fit the mood.

questions.prompt:
What is the main weakness of this description?
On my left there was a bench. On my right there was a tree. Behind me there was a fence.
options: It tours the scene, listing things without developing any of them.
questions.explanation: A list of locations gives no mood or focus. Zooming in on one detail would be stronger.

questions.prompt: Which simile best fits a calm, misty morning?
options: The mist lay over the fields like a soft grey blanket.
The mist exploded like a firework.
The mist screamed like a siren.
The mist was as loud as a drum.
questions.explanation: A soft blanket matches the stillness. The others clash with the calm mood.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the senses most effectively?
options: The kitchen smelled of burnt toast, and the radio crackled under a pile of unopened post.
There was a kitchen with things in it.
The kitchen was big and good.
questions.explanation: Smell and sound details make the scene real and hint at a slightly chaotic morning.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about descriptive writing is true or false.

statements.s: You must use all 5 senses in every paragraph.
Precise nouns and verbs often work better than extra adjectives.
A description can reveal a mood.
Piling up adjectives always makes writing stronger.

questions.explanation: Choose details and words carefully. More is not always better.

questions.prompt:
Which revision of this phrase is strongest?
the old, dark, creepy, scary house
options: the house with one shutter banging in the wind
the very old, very dark, very creepy, very scary house
the old dark creepy scary house
the house that was old and dark and creepy and scary
questions.explanation: One precise, unsettling detail does more than a pile of general adjectives.

questions.prompt: Describe a bus station at midnight. Zoom in on 2 or 3 details and develop each one. Use at least one image (simile, metaphor or personification) that fits the mood.
questions.model: The bus station hums with the sound of a single vending machine, its light flickering over an empty row of plastic seats. On the last seat, someone has left a paper cup of coffee, still steaming slightly, as if its owner might come back. Above the bays, the departures board scrolls through cancelled journeys in tired orange letters, then blinks and starts again, like someone who has told the same bad news too often.
checklist: zooms in on 2 or 3 details rather than touring
develops each detail with precise words
includes at least one fitting image
creates a clear mood
questions.explanation: Choose fewer details and say more about each.

units.title: Characters and dialogue
units.summary: Show character through what people say and do. Keep dialogue short, start a new line for each speaker, and put the punctuation inside the inverted commas.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows anger rather than telling it?
options: Sophie slammed her bag on the table and stared at the wall.
Sophie was in an angry mood.
questions.explanation: The action lets the reader work out the feeling.

questions.prompt: When should you start a new line in dialogue?
options: each time a different person speaks
only at the end of the conversation
questions.explanation: A new line for each speaker makes it clear who is talking.

questions.prompt: Which line of dialogue is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: The question mark goes inside the inverted commas, and asked continues the sentence with a small letter.
questions.misconception: Putting the question mark after the reporting clause instead of inside the inverted commas.

questions.prompt: Which reporting verb best fits a secret being shared?
questions.explanation: Whispered matches a quiet, secret moment.

questions.prompt: Which line of dialogue best shows that a character is impatient?
options: “Are we nearly there? You said 10 minutes an hour ago.”
questions.explanation: The complaint and exaggeration reveal impatience without naming it.

questions.prompt: Put this short exchange in a sensible order.
items: “Have you seen my keys?” asked Dad.
“The ones I always lose,” he sighed.
Mei pointed to the fridge. “Next to the milk again.”
questions.explanation: Each line answers the one before, and the action at the end adds humour.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about dialogue is true or false.

statements.s: Dialogue should reveal character or move the story on.
Every line of speech needs a different reporting verb.
Small actions between lines can show feelings.
Characters should explain everything to each other in long speeches.

questions.explanation: Said is often the best reporting verb, and short, purposeful dialogue works best.

questions.prompt: Which version contains a punctuation error?
options: “I'm not going,” said Callum, “unless you come too.”
questions.explanation: In the last option the question mark should be inside the inverted commas, replacing the comma.
questions.misconception: Moving the question mark outside the speech.

questions.prompt:
Which action best adds to this line?
“It's fine,” said Jordan.
options: “It's fine,” said Jordan, tearing the invitation into smaller and smaller pieces.
“It's fine,” said Jordan, and he said it.
“It's fine,” said Jordan, who was a person.
questions.explanation: The action contradicts the words, which shows Jordan is upset.

questions.prompt: Write 8 to 10 lines of dialogue in which 2 old friends meet again after a long time apart. Show how they feel through what they say and do.
questions.model:
Hannah stopped dead in the doorway of the café.
“Tomasz?”
He looked up from his phone and nearly knocked over his drink. “No way. Hannah?”
“You've grown a beard,” she said, laughing.
“You've grown taller.” He pulled out a chair. “Sit down. How long has it been?”
“Since Year 6.” She hesitated, then sat. “You never wrote back.”
Tomasz looked at the table. “I know. I'm sorry.”
“It's okay,” she said, and pushed the sugar towards him, the way she used to.
checklist: each new speaker starts a new line
speech punctuation is correct
the dialogue shows the characters' feelings
actions between lines add meaning
questions.explanation: Let the characters' words and small actions do the work.

units.title: Choosing words that fit: tone and register
units.summary: Register is how formal your writing is; tone is the attitude it carries. Choose words whose level and connotations suit your purpose and audience.

questions.prompt:
Which is the most formal word for get in this sentence?
You can get a form from reception.
questions.explanation: Obtain is formal and suits official writing.

questions.prompt: Match each informal phrase to a formal alternative.
questions.explanation: Formal writing avoids slang and phrasal verbs where a single precise word exists.

questions.prompt: Put these words in order from weakest to strongest.
questions.explanation: Each word is a stronger degree of happiness than the one before.

questions.prompt: Which sentence suits a formal letter of complaint?
options: I am writing to express my disappointment with the service I received.
Your shop is rubbish and I'm well annoyed.
OMG the service was so bad lol.
questions.explanation: It is polite and uses formal vocabulary.

questions.prompt:
What is the tone of this sentence?
Frankly, the decision to close the library is baffling.
questions.explanation: Frankly and baffling show the writer is irritated and cannot understand the decision.

questions.prompt:
Which word does NOT fit the gentle tone of this bedtime story?
The little owl ___ settled into her cosy nest.
questions.explanation: Violently clashes with the gentle, cosy mood.
questions.misconception: Choosing a word for its meaning without thinking about its connotations.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about register is true or false.

statements.s: Contractions such as don't are usually avoided in formal writing.
Slang suits a job application.
The same news can be written in a formal and an informal register.
Long words always make writing more formal and better.

questions.explanation: Register depends on audience and purpose; a word is good only if it fits.

questions.prompt:
Which sentence in this formal email slips out of register?
Dear Mrs Okafor, I am writing about the school trip. The coach was late, which was a total nightmare. I would be grateful for a refund.
options: The coach was late, which was a total nightmare.
I am writing about the school trip.
I would be grateful for a refund.
questions.explanation: Total nightmare is informal. A formal version would be: The coach was late, which caused considerable difficulty.
questions.misconception: Mixing informal phrases into an otherwise formal piece.

questions.prompt: Which word describes a thin person in the most positive way?
questions.explanation: Slender has positive connotations of grace. Scrawny and bony suggest weakness or poor health.

questions.prompt: You are late for football training. Write 2 short messages: first a text to your best friend, then a formal email to your coach, Mr Haddad. Use 2 or 3 sentences for each.
questions.model:
Text: running late!! bus never turned up, be there in 10, save me a bib x
Email: Dear Mr Haddad, I am sorry to tell you that I will be about 10 minutes late for training this evening because my bus did not arrive. I will come straight to the pitch as soon as I can. Kind regards, Fatima
checklist: the text uses an informal register suited to a friend
the email uses a formal greeting, full sentences and a sign-off
both messages give the same facts
vocabulary matches each audience
questions.explanation: Keep the facts the same and change only the register.

units.title: Argument and persuasion: making your own case
units.summary: A good argument backs a clear viewpoint with evidence and gives a fair answer to the other side. Use rhetorical devices only where they really help.

questions.prompt: What is a counter-argument?
options: the opposing view, which you state fairly and then answer
an argument you have with a friend
questions.explanation: Answering the other side shows you have thought about the issue and makes your case stronger.

questions.prompt: Which of these is evidence rather than opinion?
options: A survey of 200 pupils found that 70% wanted a longer lunch break.
Lunch breaks are far too short.
Longer lunch breaks would be amazing.
questions.explanation: A survey result can be checked. The others are judgements.

questions.prompt: Tick the 3 rhetorical devices.
questions.explanation: Rhetorical devices are choices made to persuade. Full stops and paragraphs are basic writing features.

questions.prompt: Statement: Zoos should be closed. Which is the strongest reason in favour?
options: Many large animals cannot roam as far in a zoo as they would in the wild.
My sister went to a zoo once.
Zoos are expensive for my family.
questions.explanation: It is a relevant, general reason that can be supported with evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence fairly states the other side and then answers it?
options: Some argue that zoos protect endangered species; however, this work could be done in protected wild reserves instead.
People who like zoos are wrong.
Zoos protect species, so they are good.
Nobody could possibly disagree with me.
questions.explanation: It acknowledges a real point and gives a reasoned reply.

questions.prompt: Why is it best to avoid opening an argument with Picture this...?
options: It is a stock phrase that examiners see constantly, so it sounds learned by heart.
questions.explanation: Stock openings make writing sound like a template rather than your own thinking.
questions.misconception: Believing that a memorised opening phrase guarantees a strong start.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of an argument in a sensible order.
items: a clear statement of your viewpoint
a conclusion that leaves a strong final thought
questions.explanation: Building reasons before answering the other side, then concluding, gives a logical shape.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about argument writing is true or false.

statements.s: A good argument uses evidence to support its reasons.
You should ignore the other side completely.
A rhetorical question can make the reader think.
Using as many devices as possible is always best.

questions.explanation: Evidence and fair treatment of the other side persuade more than a pile of devices.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is most effective?
options: Closing zoos would not be the end of caring for animals; it would be the start of caring for them properly.
In conclusion, that is my essay.
So zoos should close, I think, maybe.
questions.explanation: It restates the view in a memorable way using a contrast.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph arguing for or against the statement: Zoos should be closed. Include a reason, a piece of evidence, the other side's view and your answer to it.
questions.model: Zoos should not be closed, because the best of them play a vital part in saving endangered animals. Many breeding programmes, run with conservation charities, have returned animals to the wild after numbers fell to dangerously low levels. Some people argue that keeping any animal in captivity is cruel. This is a fair concern, but the answer is to raise standards in every zoo, not to close the ones that are doing important work.
checklist: states a clear viewpoint
gives a reason supported by evidence or an example
states the other side fairly
answers the other side with a reason
questions.explanation: Make sure the reply to the other side is a reason, not just a disagreement.

units.title: Speeches and talks: from notes to script
units.summary: A speech is written for the ear. Use signposts, short sentences, repetition and direct address, and speak from notes so you can look at your audience.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a signpost in a talk?
options: My second point is about cost.
questions.explanation: Signposts tell listeners where they are in the talk.

questions.prompt: Which of these is written as notes, not a script?
options: Every Saturday, a group of volunteers collects litter in the park.
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.
I would like to talk to you today about litter.
questions.explanation: Notes use key words only, so you can glance at them while speaking.

questions.prompt: Why is repetition useful in a speech?
options: Listeners cannot reread, so repeating key ideas helps them remember.
questions.explanation: Repetition helps the main message stick in the listener's mind.

questions.prompt: Which sentence works best when heard aloud?
options: Our park is full of litter. We can fix that.
It has come to our attention that the quantity of litter deposited in the park has become excessive.
Litter, which is in the park, which is a problem, is bad.
questions.explanation: Short, clear sentences are easy to follow by ear.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses direct address?
options: You can make a difference this Saturday.
questions.explanation: Speaking straight to the audience with you involves them.
questions.misconception: Thinking direct address means speaking loudly.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of a talk in a sensible order.
items: a sentence saying what the talk is about
a quick recap of the main points
questions.explanation: This shape helps listeners follow and remember the talk.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about talks is true or false.

statements.s: You should read every word from a full script without looking up.
Signposts help listeners follow the structure.
A talk should keep to one clear message.
Long, complicated sentences are easiest for listeners.

questions.explanation: Speaking from notes and keeping to the point both help an audience.

questions.prompt: Which ending best calls the audience to act?
options: So bring a pair of gloves on Saturday at 10, and let's give our park back its green.
That is the end of my talk.
questions.explanation: It tells the audience exactly what to do, when, and why.

questions.prompt:
Which version of this sentence is best for a spoken talk, and why?
A decision was taken by the committee to extend the opening hours of the library.
options: The committee has decided to keep the library open for longer.
A decision was taken by the committee, which was the library committee, to extend hours.
The library's opening hours, by committee decision, are extended.
questions.explanation: The active voice and plain words make the point quickly and clearly for listeners.

questions.prompt: Write the opening 4 or 5 sentences of a 1-minute talk persuading Year 7 pupils to join a new gardening club. Use a hook, direct address and a signpost.
questions.model: Have you ever eaten a tomato you grew yourself? If not, you are missing out. I'm Dev, and today I want to tell you about our new gardening club. First, I'll explain what we do, and then I'll tell you why it's the best hour of my week.
checklist: opens with a hook
uses direct address
includes at least one signpost
short, clear sentences suited to speaking aloud
questions.explanation: Read your opening aloud to check that it sounds natural.

units.title: Formal and informal letters
units.summary: Formal letters follow set conventions, such as matching the sign-off to the greeting; informal letters are chattier. Match your register to the person you are writing to.

questions.prompt: A formal letter begins Dear Mr Hussain. Which sign-off should it use?
questions.explanation: When you name the person, use Yours sincerely. Use Yours faithfully only after Dear Sir or Madam.

questions.prompt: In a formal letter, where does your own address go?
questions.explanation: Your address and the date go at the top right; the recipient's address goes on the left.

questions.prompt: Which opening paragraph states the purpose of a formal letter most clearly?
options: I am writing to ask whether the library could open on Sundays.
I hope the weather is nice.
My name is Ali and I like books.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph of a formal letter should say why you are writing.

questions.prompt: Match each greeting to the correct sign-off.
questions.explanation: Formal letters pair greetings and sign-offs by whether the reader is named; informal letters are personal.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is too informal for a letter to the council?
options: The park's swings are well dodgy.
The swings in the park are in poor condition.
I would be grateful if they could be repaired.
questions.explanation: Well dodgy is slang. A formal letter needs standard, polite vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of a formal letter in order from top to bottom.
questions.explanation: This layout is expected in formal letters.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about letters is true or false.

statements.s: Contractions are fine in an informal letter.
A formal letter should end with Cheers.
A formal letter should make a clear request or point.
An informal letter must include the recipient's full address.

questions.explanation: Informal letters can be chatty and need no addresses; formal letters need clear purpose and conventions.

questions.prompt:
What is wrong with this ending?
Dear Sir or Madam ... Yours sincerely, Ruby Clarke
options: It should end Yours faithfully, because the reader is not named.
questions.explanation: Dear Sir or Madam goes with Yours faithfully.
questions.misconception: Mixing up Yours sincerely and Yours faithfully.

questions.prompt: Which final paragraph is best for a formal letter asking for a new bus shelter?
options: I would be grateful if you could consider installing a shelter at the Mill Lane stop before the winter.
I hope you liked my letter about buses.
questions.explanation: It makes a clear, polite request with a sensible timescale.

questions.prompt: Write a short informal letter to a cousin who lives abroad, telling them about a recent day out. Include a greeting, 4 or 5 sentences and a friendly sign-off.
questions.model:
Dear Kofi,
You'll never guess where we went on Saturday: the giant aquarium in Plymouth! The best part was the tunnel, where sharks swam right over our heads. Ama spent the whole time pressing her nose against the glass, and she cried when we had to leave. I bought you a postcard of a turtle, so look out for it in the post. When are you visiting next?
Love from,
Efua
checklist: a friendly greeting and sign-off
a chatty, personal register
vivid details about the day out
a question or comment that speaks to the reader
questions.explanation: Write as if you are talking to someone you know well.

units.title: Articles and reviews
units.summary: A review gives a clear verdict backed by specific details, and uses article features such as a headline and standfirst to guide readers.

questions.prompt: What is a standfirst?
options: a short summary under the headline that gives the angle or verdict
the last line of an article
questions.explanation: The standfirst tells readers what to expect and hooks them in.

questions.prompt: Which is the best headline for a review of a new adventure playground?
options: Swings, slides and a rope bridge worth the wait
questions.explanation: It is short and catchy, and it hints at the verdict.

questions.prompt: Which sentence gives the most balanced judgement?
options: The rides are thrilling, although the queues can test younger visitors' patience.
questions.explanation: It balances a strength with a weakness, which makes the review more trustworthy.

questions.prompt: Which detail is the most specific?
options: The pizza arrived with a crisp base and a generous layer of melted mozzarella.
The food was nice and tasty.
I liked the food a lot.
questions.explanation: Specific details let readers judge for themselves.
questions.misconception: Thinking strong adjectives such as nice or good are enough to support a verdict.

questions.prompt: Put these parts of a review in a sensible order.
items: a paragraph saying what is being reviewed
questions.explanation: This structure guides readers from the overall verdict to the details.

questions.prompt: A review is for parents choosing a family film. Which verdict suits that audience best?
options: Funny enough for adults and gentle enough for under-8s, it's a safe choice for a family night in.
questions.explanation: It speaks to what parents need to know.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about reviews is true or false.

statements.s: A review should include the reviewer's opinion.
Retelling the whole plot is the main job of a film review.
Mentioning a weakness can make a review more convincing.
A review never needs specific examples.

questions.explanation: A review judges something, backed by examples, rather than simply retelling it.

questions.prompt:
What is the main weakness of this review paragraph?
First the hero goes to the city. Then she meets a robot. Then they fight. Then they win. Then it ends.
options: It only retells the plot and gives no judgement.
questions.explanation: A review should evaluate, not just summarise events.
questions.misconception: Confusing a review with a plot summary.

questions.prompt: Which sentence suits the register of a school magazine review?
options: The new canteen menu is a definite improvement, especially the build-your-own wraps.
Yo the food is mad now.
questions.explanation: It is lively but clear, which suits pupils and staff reading a school magazine.

questions.prompt: Write 2 paragraphs reviewing a park, café or attraction you know. Include specific details, one strength, one weakness and a clear verdict.
questions.model:
Riverside Park has had a makeover, and most of it is a success. The new playground has a rope bridge, a zip wire and soft flooring, and on a sunny Saturday it is full of families. The best addition is the small café by the pond, which sells hot chocolate for under 2 pounds.
However, there are only 2 toilets, and the queue can be long. Overall, Riverside Park is well worth a visit for families with young children, as long as you plan ahead.
checklist: specific details about the place
at least one strength and one weakness
a clear overall verdict
a register suited to readers of a review
questions.explanation: Back every judgement with a detail.

units.title: Writing an analytical essay
units.summary: An analytical essay answers a question with a clear argument, supported by short quotations and close analysis, in a formal register and the present tense.

questions.prompt: Question: How does Dickens present Scrooge as cut off from other people? Which is the best one-sentence argument?
options: Dickens presents Scrooge as a man so cold and mean that everyone, even animals, keeps away, and he likes it that way.
Scrooge is a character in a book.
Dickens wrote A Christmas Carol in 1843.
questions.explanation: A strong argument answers the question directly and sets up the ideas the essay will develop.

questions.prompt: Which tense should you use when writing about what happens in a text?
options: any tense, as long as you vary it
questions.explanation: Literary analysis uses the present tense because the text is always there to be read.
questions.misconception: Switching to the past tense because the text was written long ago.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best supports the point that people avoid Scrooge?
options: “Nobody ever stopped him in the street”
“Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grind-stone”
“A frosty rime was on his head”
“External heat and cold had little influence on Scrooge”
questions.explanation: It directly shows that nobody approaches him.

questions.prompt: Put the parts of an analytical essay in order.
items: an introduction that states your argument
a main paragraph on the first idea
a main paragraph on the second idea
a main paragraph on the third idea
a conclusion with your overall judgement
questions.explanation: Each main paragraph develops one idea that supports the argument.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best?
options: Dickens makes Scrooge's isolation complete, and because Scrooge chooses it, his later change will seem all the more remarkable.
In conclusion, I have written about Scrooge.
In conclusion, Scrooge is mean, cold, avoided and likes it.
That is the end of my essay.
questions.explanation: It reaches a judgement and looks at the bigger picture rather than repeating every point.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is too informal for an analytical essay?
options: Scrooge is well tight with his money.
Scrooge is extremely mean with money.
The list of verbs emphasises Scrooge's greed.
questions.explanation: Well tight is slang. Essays need a formal register.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses a literary term accurately?
options: The simile “solitary as an oyster” suggests Scrooge shuts himself away like a shellfish in its shell.
The metaphor “solitary as an oyster” shows Scrooge likes the sea.
The onomatopoeia “solitary as an oyster” makes a sound.
The alliteration “solitary as an oyster” rhymes.
questions.explanation: As shows this is a simile, and the comment explains what the comparison suggests.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about essays is true or false.

statements.s: Each main paragraph should focus on one idea.
Long quotations are better than short ones.
The introduction should answer the question.
You should retell the whole story before analysing it.

questions.explanation: Focused paragraphs built on short quotations make an essay strong.

questions.prompt: Which topic sentence links most clearly back to the question about Scrooge being cut off from others?
options: Even animals sense Scrooge's coldness, which shows how complete his isolation is.
questions.explanation: It makes a point that directly answers the question.

questions.prompt: Write an introduction and one main paragraph for the essay: How does Dickens present Scrooge as cut off from other people?
questions.model:
Introduction: Dickens presents Scrooge as a man who is completely cut off from other people, and who has chosen to be. His coldness keeps everyone away, and Dickens suggests that this isolation is the very thing Scrooge enjoys.
Main paragraph: Dickens shows that no one approaches Scrooge at all. “Nobody ever stopped him in the street” to greet him, and even beggars and children avoid him. Most strikingly, “the blind men’s dogs” pull their owners into doorways when they see him, a comic exaggeration which suggests that even animals sense his coldness. Yet Scrooge does not mind: being avoided is “the very thing he liked”, which makes his isolation a choice rather than a misfortune.
checklist: an introduction that states a clear argument
a main paragraph with one clear idea
short, embedded quotations with close analysis
formal register and the present tense
questions.explanation: Keep linking your analysis back to the question.

units.title: Drafting, editing and proofreading
units.summary: Editing improves the writing; proofreading corrects errors. Read your work aloud and check for one kind of error at a time.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between editing and proofreading?
options: Editing improves the writing; proofreading corrects errors such as spelling and punctuation.
Proofreading changes the story; editing only checks spelling.
questions.explanation: Edit for quality and structure first, then proofread for accuracy.
questions.misconception: Thinking that checking spelling is all that improving a draft involves.

questions.prompt:
Which word is spelt wrongly in this sentence?
The weather was beautifull on the first day of the holiday.
questions.explanation: The suffix -ful has only one l: beautiful.

questions.prompt:
Which word should replace the mistake in this sentence?
The pupils left there coats in the hall.
questions.explanation: Their shows belonging: their coats.

questions.prompt:
Which version correctly fixes the comma splice?
The rain stopped, we went outside.
options: The rain stopped, so we went outside.
The rain stopped, we, went outside.
The rain, stopped we went outside.
The rain stopped we went outside.
questions.explanation: Adding the conjunction so joins the 2 main clauses correctly.

questions.prompt:
Tick the 3 errors in this sentence.
me and my freind could of won the race.
questions.explanation: It should read: My friend and I could have won the race. Me and my should be My friend and I, freind is misspelt, and could of should be could have.

questions.prompt:
Which edit best improves this sentence?
Then we went to the shop and then we went to the park and then we went home.
options: After a quick stop at the shop, we spent an hour in the park before heading home.
Then we went to the shop, then the park, then home, and then that was it.
We went to the shop and then the park and then home.
Then, then, then we went home.
questions.explanation: It removes the repeated and then and varies the sentence structure.

questions.prompt:
Which revision makes this sentence suitable for a letter to a headteacher?
The new timetable is pretty rubbish to be honest.
options: Many pupils feel the new timetable could be improved.
The new timetable is pretty rubbish.
To be honest, the timetable is rubbish.
The new timetable is well bad.
questions.explanation: It keeps the meaning but uses a polite, formal register suited to the audience.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about proofreading is true or false.

statements.s: Reading your work aloud can help you spot errors.
A spellchecker catches every mistake.
It helps to check for one kind of error at a time.
Proofreading should only be done by a teacher.

questions.explanation: Spellcheckers miss homophones such as there and their, so careful rereading matters.

questions.prompt:
Which correction is right?
We should of left earlier.
questions.explanation: Should of comes from mishearing should've. The correct form is should have.
questions.misconception: Writing of instead of have after should, could or would.

questions.prompt:
Proofread and edit this paragraph. Correct the errors and improve the style.
the bus was late again, everyone was annoyed. it was raining and it was cold and it was dark. jess said its always like this, she was right.
questions.model: The bus was late again, and everyone was annoyed. Rain fell steadily from a dark, freezing sky. “It’s always like this,” Jess muttered, and she was right.
checklist: capital letters at the start of each sentence and for Jess
comma splices corrected
its corrected to it's (or the speech set out correctly)
the repetitive sentence improved
questions.explanation: Correct every error, then improve the sentence that repeats it was.

units.title: Word classes revisited
units.summary: A word's class depends on the job it does in the sentence. The national curriculum calls my, your and their determiners, and mine, yours and theirs possessive pronouns.

questions.prompt:
What is the word class of quickly in this sentence?
The fox ran quickly across the field.
questions.explanation: Quickly tells us how the fox ran, so it is an adverb modifying the verb.

questions.prompt:
Which word in this sentence is a noun?
Her courage surprised everyone.
questions.explanation: Courage names an idea, so it is an abstract noun. Her is a determiner, surprised is a verb and everyone is a pronoun.

questions.prompt:
Tick the 3 determiners in this sentence.
Our neighbours painted their fence this weekend.
questions.explanation: Our, their and this all come before a noun to specify it. The national curriculum glossary lists possessives such as our and their as determiners.
questions.misconception: Calling our and their possessive pronouns, although they come before a noun and work as determiners.

questions.prompt:
What is the word class of mine in this sentence?
The blue bag is mine.
questions.explanation: Mine stands on its own in place of a noun phrase (my bag), so it is a possessive pronoun.

questions.prompt:
What job does might do in this sentence?
We might visit Leeds next week.
options: It is a modal verb showing possibility.
It is a noun meaning strength.
questions.explanation: Might is a modal verb. Here it shows that the visit is possible but not certain.

questions.prompt: Match each word to its word class.
questions.explanation: Beneath shows position, although introduces a subordinate clause, perhaps shows how likely something is, and those specifies a noun.

questions.prompt: Write the adjective formed from the noun danger.
questions.explanation: Adding the suffix -ous turns the noun danger into the adjective dangerous.

questions.prompt: Sam says after is always a preposition. Which sentence proves him wrong, because after is a subordinating conjunction there?
questions.explanation: In After we ate, after introduces a clause with its own verb (ate). After lunch is a preposition phrase.
questions.misconception: Thinking a word always belongs to the same class, whatever job it does.

questions.prompt:
Lucy thinks fast must be an adjective because it does not end in -ly. What is its word class in this sentence, and why?
She ran fast.
options: adverb, because it tells us how she ran
noun, because it names a thing
verb, because it is an action
questions.explanation: Fast tells us how she ran, so here it is an adverb. In a fast car it would be an adjective.
questions.misconception: Assuming only words ending in -ly can be adverbs.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about word classes is true or false.

statements.s: A word's class depends on how it is used in a sentence.
In the national curriculum glossary, my is a pronoun.
Might and must are modal verbs.
Every word ending in -ly is an adverb.

questions.explanation: My is a determiner in the glossary. Words such as friendly and lovely end in -ly but are adjectives.

units.title: Phrases and clauses
units.summary: A phrase is built around a head word, such as the noun in a noun phrase. A clause is built around a verb; a main clause can stand alone, and a subordinate clause depends on it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a clause?
questions.explanation: The dog barked has a subject and a verb. The others are phrases.

questions.prompt:
What is the head word of this noun phrase?
the old lighthouse on the cliff
questions.explanation: Everything else in the phrase adds information about the lighthouse, so it is the head.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a preposition phrase?
questions.explanation: A preposition phrase is headed by a preposition, here under.

questions.prompt:
Write the subordinating conjunction in this sentence.
We waited until the rain stopped.
questions.explanation: Until introduces the subordinate clause until the rain stopped.

questions.prompt:
Which words form the relative clause?
The painting, which hung in the hall, was stolen.
questions.explanation: The relative clause begins with which and adds information about the painting.

questions.prompt:
Which words form the main clause?
When the bell rang, the pupils filed out.
questions.explanation: The pupils filed out can stand alone. When the bell rang depends on it.

questions.prompt:
Ola says this sentence has no relative clause because there is no who, which or that. Which words show she is wrong?
The book I borrowed was brilliant.
questions.explanation: The relative pronoun has been left out: The book (that) I borrowed was brilliant.
questions.misconception: Thinking a relative clause must begin with who, which or that.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: A phrase can never contain a verb.
A subordinate clause can come at the start of a sentence.
A main clause can stand alone as a sentence.
Every relative clause begins with who.

questions.explanation: The national curriculum defines a phrase by its head word: the noun phrase the boy who lives next door contains the verb lives. Relative clauses can also begin with which, where, whose or that.
questions.misconception: Learning the shortcut that a phrase has no verb, which does not match the national curriculum definition.

questions.prompt: Which is the most fully expanded noun phrase, and why?
options: a small, battered suitcase with a broken handle: it adds words before and after the head noun
a suitcase: it is short and clear
the suitcase was battered: it has a verb
questions.explanation: It has adjectives before the noun and a preposition phrase after it, all built around suitcase.

questions.prompt: Which sentence contains both a relative clause and a subordinate clause introduced by a subordinating conjunction?
options: Because it was late, the girl who lives next door walked home with us.
The girl walked home with us.
The girl who lives next door walked home.
Because it was late, we walked home.
questions.explanation: Because it was late is a subordinate clause; who lives next door is a relative clause.

units.title: Sentence functions and sentence forms
units.summary: The 4 sentence functions are statement, question, command and exclamation; in grammar, an exclamation begins with What or How. Single-clause and multi-clause describe how a sentence is built.

questions.prompt:
What is the function of this sentence?
Close the window, please.
questions.explanation: It tells someone to do something, so it is a command, even with please.

questions.prompt:
What is the function of this sentence?
Have you finished your homework?
questions.explanation: It asks for information, and the verb have comes before the subject you.

questions.prompt: Match each sentence to its function.
pairs: What a view we had from the top!
questions.explanation: The function depends on the sentence's grammar, not only its end punctuation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an exclamation in the grammatical sense?
options: How tall that tree has grown!
questions.explanation: It begins with How and has a subject (that tree) and a verb (has grown).
questions.misconception: Thinking any sentence ending in an exclamation mark is an exclamation.

questions.prompt:
Jade says this sentence must be multi-clause because it is so long. Is she right, and why?
The enormous grey whale surfaced slowly beside our small boat.
options: No: it has only one verb, so it is single-clause.
Yes: long sentences are always multi-clause.
No: it is not a sentence at all.
questions.explanation: It is long, but it has only one verb (surfaced), so it is a single-clause sentence.
questions.misconception: Assuming a long sentence must be multi-clause.

questions.prompt:
How is this sentence built?
I stayed in, but my sister went out.
options: a multi-clause sentence with 2 main clauses joined by a co-ordinating conjunction
a multi-clause sentence with a relative clause
questions.explanation: But joins 2 main clauses that could each stand alone. This is sometimes called a compound sentence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is multi-clause with a subordinate clause?
options: Although it was snowing, the match went ahead.
Snow fell and the match went ahead.
questions.explanation: Although it was snowing is a subordinate clause attached to the main clause. This is sometimes called a complex sentence.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: A command can end with a full stop.
A statement ending in an exclamation mark becomes an exclamation.
A question can begin with a question word such as where.
A single-clause sentence must be short.

questions.explanation: Function depends on grammar, and a single-clause sentence can be long if it has only one clause.

questions.prompt:
Which change turns this statement into an exclamation in the grammatical sense?
The view is beautiful.
questions.explanation: Starting with How and keeping the subject and verb (the view is) makes a grammatical exclamation.

questions.prompt:
Which description of this sentence is correct?
Although the path was steep, we reached the top before dark.
options: It is multi-clause: a subordinate clause comes first, followed by the main clause.
It is single-clause because it has one full stop.
It has 2 main clauses joined by and.
questions.explanation: Although the path was steep is the subordinate clause; we reached the top before dark is the main clause.

units.title: Varying sentences for effect
units.summary: Vary the length and openings of your sentences on purpose. A short sentence after long ones gives emphasis; holding back a key word builds suspense.

questions.prompt: Which sentence begins with a fronted adverbial?
options: Without a word, Mo left the room.
Mo left the room without a word.
questions.explanation: Without a word tells us how Mo left and has been moved to the front, followed by a comma.

questions.prompt: Which sentence opens with a verb ending in -ing?
options: Shivering, Tom pulled his coat tighter.
Tom pulled his coat tighter because he was shivering.
questions.explanation: Opening with Shivering puts the feeling first and varies the usual subject-first pattern.

questions.prompt: Which sentence holds back the most important word until the end?
options: Inside the box, wrapped in silk, was a key.
A key was inside the box, wrapped in silk.
The key was in the box.
There was a key in a silk box.
questions.explanation: The reader waits through 2 phrases before discovering the key, which builds curiosity.

questions.prompt: What is the usual effect of a short sentence after several long ones?
options: It gives emphasis, making the idea land hard.
It shows the writer ran out of ideas.
questions.explanation: The contrast in length draws attention to the short sentence.

questions.prompt: Put these sentences in the order that builds the most tension, ending with the short one.
items: The corridor stretched ahead, lit only by the green glow of the exit sign.
Somewhere behind her, a door clicked shut.
questions.explanation: The sentences grow shorter as the tension rises, ending on a single word.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: When the music stopped, everyone froze.
When the music stopped everyone, froze.
When, the music stopped everyone froze.
When the music, stopped everyone froze.
questions.explanation: Put a comma after a subordinate clause at the start of a sentence.

questions.prompt: Which version varies the sentence openings best?
options: Slowly, the train pulled away. Through the window, Ruby watched the platform shrink. She did not wave.
Ruby got on the train. Ruby sat down. Ruby looked out. Ruby did not wave.
The train left. The platform shrank. The girl watched. The girl did not wave.
Ruby got on the train and sat down and looked out and did not wave.
questions.explanation: It opens with an adverb, then an adverbial phrase, then the subject, and ends with a short sentence.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Every sentence in a paragraph should be the same length.
A fronted adverbial is usually followed by a comma.
Moving a key word to the end of a sentence can create suspense.
Starting every sentence with the subject keeps writing lively.

questions.explanation: Deliberate variety keeps writing interesting; starting every sentence the same way soon becomes dull.
questions.misconception: Thinking that varied sentences means making them all long and complicated.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a rhetorical question that would suit a persuasive speech about a polluted river?
options: Would you swim in water this filthy?
What time does the river close?
Has anyone got a map of the river?
questions.explanation: A rhetorical question expects no answer and makes listeners think about the issue.

questions.prompt:
Which revision of this paragraph best varies length, openings and order?
I walked into the hall. I saw the stage. I felt nervous. I walked to the piano.
options: The hall was silent. As I crossed to the piano, every footstep echoed off the stage. My hands were shaking.
I walked into the hall and I saw the stage and I felt nervous and I walked to the piano.
I walked. I saw. I felt. I walked.
I walked into the hall, I saw the stage, I felt nervous, I walked to the piano.
questions.explanation: It mixes a short opening, a sentence starting with a subordinate clause, and a final short sentence, while showing the nerves.

units.title: Full stops, capital letters and the comma splice
